evidence.snippet: Interestingly, none of the mutations prevent folding or oligomerization of recombinant fragments containing the mutations in vitro. Instead, they prevent Ca(2+) binding by the carbohydrate-recognition domains of CL-K1.
evidence.explanation: Recombinant fragments carrying Ser169Pro, Gly204Ser or Ser217 deletion lose calcium binding. Refolding in vitro does not exclude a biosynthetic folding defect in cells.

steps/3.description: Three tested COLEC11 carbohydrate-recognition-domain variants (Ser169Pro, Gly204Ser and Ser217 deletion) abolish calcium binding in recombinant fragments. The fragments can refold and oligomerize in vitro, but lack calcium-dependent stabilization.

evidence.snippet: Both full-length CL-K1 and the wild-type fragment bound to the invertase, but the three variant fragments did not bind (Figure 6C).
evidence.explanation: The assay directly measures loss of carbohydrate recognition in the recombinant variants. The corresponding developmental ligand has not been established.

steps/4.description: Recombinant CL-K1 fragments carrying the three tested 3MC-associated carbohydrate-recognition-domain variants fail to bind yeast invertase or the dextran chromatography matrix. These ligand-binding assays demonstrate functional loss even though the fragments assemble into trimers in vitro.

evidence.snippet: We also demonstrate that three disease-associated mutations prevent secretion of CL-K1 from mammalian cells, accounting for the protein deficiency observed in patients.
evidence.explanation: The three tested COLEC11 carbohydrate-recognition-domain variants block secretion in the mammalian expression assay.

evidence.snippet: Using western blotting, we failed to detect any secreted CL-K1 in the serum of two patients (Gly204Ser), in contrast to control samples
evidence.explanation: Two affected individuals lacked detectable serum CL-K1. Intracellular retention was suggested, not directly measured in these patients.

steps/5.description: Biallelic COLEC11 loss-of-function variants reduce functional extracellular CL-K1. Three tested carbohydrate-recognition-domain variants block secretion in mammalian cells, and Gly204Ser CL-K1 was undetectable in serum from two patients. This node does not assume that all COLEC11 variants share the same biosynthetic defect.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate how mutations in COLEC10 (c.25C>T; p.Arg9Ter, c.226delA; p.Gly77Glufs*66 and c.528C>G p.Cys176Trp) impair the expression and/or secretion of CL-L1 highlighting their pathogenicity.
evidence.explanation: The tested truncating alleles eliminate detectable expressed protein; Cys176Trp permits intracellular expression but markedly reduces secretion.

steps/6.description: Some biallelic COLEC10 variants impair CL-L1 expression or secretion. Arg9Ter and Gly77Glufs*66 constructs yield no detectable protein, whereas Cys176Trp accumulates intracellularly with severely reduced secretion. This route is distinct from the Cys270Serfs*33 allele, which has normal measured plasma levels but impaired chemoattractant activity.

evidence.snippet: Plasma levels of CL-L1 in the patient and her parents were within normal range, suggesting that this variant does not modify transcription or secretion.
evidence.explanation: Measured plasma abundance was normal in the Cys270Serfs*33 family; abundance alone does not demonstrate every step of transcription or secretion.

evidence.snippet: However, the variant affects the chemo-attractive feature of CL-L1, as HeLa cells migrate significantly less in response to the mutant protein compared to the wild-type one.
evidence.explanation: The mutant protein has reduced chemoattractant activity in HeLa cells; the assay does not directly test neural crest cells.

steps/7.description: The homozygous COLEC10 c.807_810delCTGT (p.Cys270Serfs*33) variant extends the protein and removes a conserved cysteine. Plasma CL-L1 levels were normal in the reported family, while mutant protein induced less HeLa-cell migration than wild type. Loss of extracellular function can therefore occur without reduced measured abundance.

evidence.snippet: We characterized the naturally occurring 3MC-associated MASP-3 mutants and found that they all yielded enzymatically inactive proteins.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that the 3MC-associated MASP1 alleles abolish MASP-3 catalytic activity.

steps/8.description: Biallelic MASP1 variants impair MASP-3 serine protease activity. Tested 3MC-associated MASP-3 mutants were enzymatically inactive. Variants confined to the exon-12 protease domain can selectively affect MASP-3, whereas earlier truncating variants may also affect MASP-1 or MAp44; selective MASP-3 deficiency is not assumed for every genotype.

evidence.snippet: although 3MC patients predominantly contain pro-FD, they also contain detectable levels of mature FD
evidence.explanation: Patient samples demonstrate incomplete maturation. Residual mature factor D does not by itself establish normal alternative-pathway activity or absence of clinical infection risk.

evidence.snippet: For this study we evolved a specific MASP-3 inhibitor and unambiguously proved that activated MASP-3 is the exclusive pro-FD activator in resting blood, which demonstrates a fundamental link between the lectin and alternative pathways.
evidence.explanation: Selective inhibitor experiments in resting human plasma establish the role of activated MASP-3 under the tested conditions. The paper distinguishes this from coagulated serum, where other proteases may contribute.

steps/9.description: MASP-3 deficiency compromises conversion of pro-factor D to mature factor D. Tested patient samples predominantly contain pro-factor D but retain detectable mature factor D, consistent with an additional maturation route. Resting-plasma inhibition experiments establish MASP-3 dependence under those assay conditions; serum coagulation and patient measurements need separate interpretation.

evidence.snippet: At 24 hpf, the organisation of streaming NCC through the somites is severely disrupted in the colec11 morphants and obviously truncated in the masp1 morphants
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish morpholino perturbations alter neural crest distribution and streaming. The masp1 perturbation does not isolate MASP-3 from other gene products.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we injected SOX10-eGFP zebrafish with colec11 and masp1 MO and observed at 48 hpf, ectopic NCC in the head, trunk and periphery
evidence.explanation: Ectopic neural crest cells support dysregulated guidance rather than a uniform decrease in cell number.

steps/10.description: Experimental colec11 or masp1 knockdown causes ectopic neural crest distribution and disrupted migratory streams in zebrafish. Recombinant CL-K1 also attracts quail neural crest cells in explants. These observations support a guidance defect as a candidate cause of craniofacial malformation in 3MC; they do not establish that every affected organ derives from neural crest.

evidence.snippet: CL-11 deletion resulted in marked impairment of OCL differentiation, which was partially rescued by supplementation of the differentiation medium with recombinant CL-11.
evidence.explanation: Engineered healthy-donor human iPSC-derived cells establish a cellular requirement and partial rescue, not a patient skeletal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: By comparison, OCLs derived from Colec11−/− SKO mice exhibited only modest reductions in OCL number and size
evidence.explanation: Single-gene mouse deficiency has a mild cellular effect despite its low frequency of overt spinal curvature.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, Colec11−/−/C3−/− BMSCs exhibited pronounced reduction in multinucleated OCL formation, quantified by the microscopic area occupied by such cells
evidence.explanation: The cellular readout is TRAP-positive multinucleated osteoclast formation/area, not a direct bone-resorption assay.

evidence.snippet: In addition, treatment with Mirococept—a truncated complement receptor-1–based inhibitor of C3 and C5 convertases (23)—significantly reduced OCL formation, demonstrating that normal human OCL differentiation is complement-dependent.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacologic C3/C5 convertase inhibition supports complement involvement; it is not a C3 gene-deletion experiment or proof that a specific linear complement sequence is necessary.

steps/11.description: Experimental loss of collectin-11 impairs osteoclast differentiation in mouse bone-marrow cultures and engineered healthy-donor human iPSC-derived cells. The effect is modest after isolated mouse Colec11 deletion and pronounced in Colec11/C3 or Colec11/Cfb double-knockout cultures; isolated human COLEC11 deletion already has a marked effect. Recombinant CL-11 partially rescues differentiation, and complement-convertase inhibition impairs differentiation in human cells. These results identify a candidate mechanism relevant to 3MC, without establishing osteoclast dysfunction as the cause of skeletal malformations in affected patients.

evidence.snippet: Striking differences in the craniofacial skeleton were observed compared with uninjected/standard morpholino injected embryos, such as reduced mandibular length (e.g. shortened Meckel and palatoquadrate cartilages), malformation of the anterior neurocranium with shortening of the trabeculae and the ethmoid plate, shortening and abnormal angulation of the ceratohyal cartilage
evidence.explanation: Perturbed zebrafish CL-K1 expression causes craniofacial cartilage defects.

steps/12.description: Craniofacial cartilage and bone development is disrupted in zebrafish models, supporting a developmental explanation for the facial abnormalities and clefting of 3MC. Expression of CL-K1 and CL-L1 in murine palatal and craniofacial tissues supports biological plausibility, without proving a specific mechanism for each human malformation.

evidence.snippet: Type I ADCA can be further divided based on the proposed pathogenetic mechanism into 3 subclasses: subclass 1 includes type I ADCA caused by CAG repeat expansions such as SCA1-SCA3, SCA17, and DRPLA, subclass 2 includes trinucleotide repeat expansions that fall outside of the protein-coding regions of the disease gene including SCA8, SCA10 and SCA12. Subclass 3 contains disorders caused by specific gene deletions, missense mutation, and nonsense mutation and includes SCA13, SCA14, SCA15/16, SCA27 and SCA28.
evidence.explanation: Establishes three mechanistically different branches within the historical ADCA-I phenotype class.

steps/20.description: ADCA-I is unified by a dominant ataxia-plus phenotype, not by one proximal lesion. Coding polyglutamine expansions, other coding or noncoding repeat expansions, and conventional sequence or copy-number variants initiate distinct molecular cascades that converge on cerebellar and variably extracerebellar neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: these syndromes is that the polyglutamine product is in some way toxic to the cell at the protein level.
evidence.explanation: Supports protein-level toxic gain of function in the polyglutamine subclass without extending that mechanism to all ADCA-I subtypes.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disease caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the TATA-box binding protein gene (TBP).
evidence.explanation: Documents the CAG repeat-expansion gain-of-function lesion in the representative ADCA-I subtype SCA17.

steps/21.description: In SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA17, and DRPLA, coding CAG expansions lengthen a polyglutamine tract. The expanded proteins alter native interactions, protein quality control, transcription, and calcium homeostasis. Repeat instability can also produce anticipation and repeat-length-dependent age at onset in these subtypes.

evidence.snippet: subclass 2 includes trinucleotide repeat expansions that fall outside of the protein-coding regions of the disease gene including SCA8, SCA10 and SCA12.
evidence.explanation: Supports a distinct historical noncoding-repeat subclass.

evidence.snippet: we identified a heterozygous GGC-repeat expansion in a large Utah pedigree encoding polyglycine (polyG) in zinc finger homeobox protein 3 (ZFHX3), also known as AT-binding transcription factor 1 (ATBF1).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the coding polyglycine-repeat lesion in SCA4.

evidence.snippet: In fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cells, the GGC expansion led to increased ZFHX3 protein levels and abnormal autophagy, which were normalized with small interfering RNA-mediated ZFHX3 knockdown in both cell types.
evidence.explanation: Links expanded ZFHX3 to abnormal autophagy in human cellular models.

steps/22.description: This branch includes noncoding repeat expansions with RNA-mediated or repeat-associated mechanisms and coding repeats that yield non-polyglutamine proteins. SCA4 is now known to arise from a coding GGC expansion in ZFHX3; the resulting polyglycine protein aggregates and abnormal autophagy provide a concrete example. The branch does not imply that all noncoding repeat diseases share the SCA4 mechanism. Two further ADCA-I subtypes belong here: SCA12 arises from a CAG expansion outside the PPP2R2B coding sequence, and SCA37 from an (ATTTC)n pentanucleotide insertion in a noncoding region of DAB1.

evidence.snippet: Subclass 3 contains disorders caused by specific gene deletions, missense mutation, and nonsense mutation and includes SCA13, SCA14, SCA15/16, SCA27 and SCA28.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the repeat-independent conventional-variant branch.

steps/23.description: ADCA-I also includes repeat-independent disorders caused by missense, nonsense, or deletion variants whose molecular mechanism is not established. This node carries those: TMEM240 (SCA21), TGM6 (SCA35, a disputed gene-disease relationship) and CCDC88C (SCA40). The conventional-variant subtypes whose mechanism *is* known have their own nodes: PRKCG and ITPR1 on the Purkinje-cell calcium signaling node, KCNC3, KCND3 and FGF14 on the ion channel node, AFG3L2 and PNPT1 on the two mitochondrial nodes, and ELOVL4 on the very-long-chain fatty acid node.

evidence.snippet: the dramatic effects of altering protein conformations on neuronal function and survival
evidence.explanation: This review of trinucleotide-repeat disorders identifies altered protein conformation as a key driver of impaired neuronal function and survival, supporting misfolded-protein aggregation and proteostatic stress as a core ADCA-I disease mechanism.

steps/24.description: Expanded polyglutamine ataxin-1, ataxin-2, and TBP adopt aberrant conformations and form nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. Sequestration of chaperones, ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy components, and interacting partners progressively impairs neuronal proteostasis, contributing to Purkinje-cell and brainstem-neuron dysfunction. This proteostatic stress is a convergent downstream consequence of the polyglutamine subtypes and is described mechanistically here without an independent ADCA-I-specific quantitative claim.

evidence.snippet: neurodegenerative disease caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the TATA-box binding protein gene (TBP)
evidence.explanation: In the representative ADCA-I subtype SCA17 the causative gene is TBP, the TATA-box binding protein — the general RNA polymerase II transcription initiation factor. A polyglutamine-encoding CAG expansion in TBP places the disease lesion directly within the core transcription machinery, mechanistically grounding transcriptional dysregulation as a shared nuclear ADCA-I mechanism.

steps/25.description: Several ADCA-I proteins act in the nucleus: TBP is a core general transcription factor and expanded ataxin-1 reorganizes native transcriptional regulator complexes (e.g., with CIC and RBM17), skewing gene-expression programs required for Purkinje-cell homeostasis. Transcriptional dysregulation is a shared nuclear mechanism among the polyglutamine ADCA-I subtypes; subtype-specific molecular detail is left for follow-up curation of the individual subtype entries. One non-polyglutamine subtype also belongs here: CAMTA1, mutated in the nonprogressive congenital ataxia that Orphanet classifies under ADCA-I, encodes a calmodulin-binding transcription activator.

evidence.snippet: Several forms of SCAs are caused by missense mutations or deletions in genes related to calcium signaling in Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: States the shared calcium-signaling theme this node groups.

evidence.snippet: IP3R1, CAR8 and PKCγ proteins are strongly and specifically expressed in Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: Sources the Purkinje-cell specificity of the two proteins bound on this node.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor type 1 gene (ITPR1) lead to SCA15, SCA16, and SCA29.
evidence.explanation: Assigns ITPR1 to the dominant ataxias represented on this node.

evidence.snippet: PKCγ dysregulation causes abnormal Purkinje cell dendritic development and SCA14.
evidence.explanation: Bridges PRKCG dysfunction to Purkinje-cell dendritic pathology, the mechanism this node states.

steps/26.description: Several conventional-variant ADCA-I subtypes disturb calcium handling in Purkinje cells. PRKCG (SCA14) encodes protein kinase C gamma and ITPR1 (SCA29, and also SCA15/16) encodes the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor; both are strongly and specifically expressed in Purkinje cells and act in the same calcium-regulatory pathway, which also controls Purkinje dendritic development.

evidence.snippet: The voltage-dependent potassium channel subunit Kv3.3 is expressed at high levels in cerebellar Purkinje cells, in auditory brainstem nuclei and in many other neurons capable of firing at high rates.
evidence.explanation: Sources the Purkinje-cell localisation and high-frequency firing role of Kv3.3 asserted by this node.

evidence.snippet: human mutations in the gene encoding Kv3.3 (KCNC3) result in a unique neurodegenerative disease termed spinocerebellar ataxia type 13 (SCA13).
evidence.explanation: Links KCNC3 channel dysfunction to a dominant cerebellar degeneration.

evidence.snippet: SCA19/22 is caused by variants in the KCND3 gene, which encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel subunit essential for cerebellar Purkinje cell function.
evidence.explanation: Links KCND3 channel dysfunction to a dominant cerebellar ataxia and names its Purkinje-cell role.

evidence.snippet: When overexpressed, KV4.3S357W channels alone showed no current.
evidence.explanation: Functional demonstration that an SCA19/22 variant abolishes the potassium current.

steps/27.description: Three conventional-variant ADCA-I subtypes converge on the excitability of cerebellar Purkinje cells. KCNC3 (SCA13) and KCND3 (SCA19/22) encode the Kv3.3 and Kv4.3 potassium channel subunits; FGF14 (SCA27A) encodes an intracellular fibroblast growth factor that modulates neuronal sodium channels. Loss or alteration of these channel functions disturbs the high-frequency firing pattern that Purkinje cells depend on.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the AFG3L2 gene have been linked to spinocerebellar ataxia type 28 and spastic ataxia-neuropathy syndrome in humans; however, the pathogenic mechanism is still unclear.
evidence.explanation: Links AFG3L2 to SCA28 in humans.

evidence.snippet: Examination of PCs prior to neurodegeneration revealed fragmentation and altered distribution of mitochondria in the dendritic tree, indicating that abnormal mitochondrial dynamics is an early event in the pathogenic process.
evidence.explanation: Sources the early mitochondrial fragmentation in Purkinje cells described by this node.

evidence.snippet: To unravel the underlying mechanism, we examined a constitutive knockout of Afg3l2, which revealed a decreased rate of mitochondrial protein synthesis associated with impaired mitochondrial ribosome assembly.
evidence.explanation: Sources the fall in mitochondrial protein synthesis described by this node.

steps/28.description: AFG3L2 (SCA28) is a subunit of the mitochondrial m-AAA protease, which degrades misfolded inner-membrane proteins and processes specific substrates. In a conditional mouse model, Purkinje-cell deletion of Afg3l2 caused mitochondrial fragmentation in the dendritic tree, and a constitutive knockout lowered the rate of mitochondrial protein synthesis through impaired mitoribosome assembly.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 25 (SCA25) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the PNPT1 gene, primarily affecting the critical S1 RNA-binding domain.
evidence.explanation: Assigns PNPT1, a mitochondrial RNA-processing enzyme, to SCA25 and names the affected domain.

evidence.snippet: Finally, overexpression of the wild-type PNPT1 cDNA in fibroblasts of subject 1 induced an increase in 5S rRNA import in mitochondria and rescued the mitochondrial-translation deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that PNPT1 acts on RNA import into mitochondria, the mitochondrial role this node's name and description assert. Recessive PNPT1 variants give a separate respiratory-chain disease; this item is cited for the gene's function, not for the SCA25 phenotype.

steps/29.description: PNPT1 (SCA25) encodes polyribonucleotide nucleotidyltransferase 1, which acts in mitochondrial RNA metabolism; the reported pathogenic variants cluster in its S1 RNA-binding domain. This is a separate mechanism from the AFG3L2 protease defect, sharing only the organelle, and the SCA25 phenotype couples cerebellar ataxia with a prominent sensory neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal dominant variants in ELOVL4 cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 34 (SCA34; ATX-ELOVL4), classically associated with a skin condition known as erythrokeratoderma.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ELOVL4 as the SCA34 gene.

evidence.snippet: Of note, skin lesions related to erythrokeratoderma were seen in a minority of cases (33.3%).
evidence.explanation: Sources the statement that erythrokeratoderma is present in only a minority of reported cases.

steps/30.description: ELOVL4 (SCA34) encodes the elongase that makes very-long-chain fatty acids. Dominant ELOVL4 variants cause a progressive ataxia in which cerebellar atrophy is essentially universal on imaging, classically accompanied by erythrokeratoderma, although the skin lesion is present in only a minority of reported cases. Other ELOVL4 alleles instead cause a retinal maculopathy, so the tissue affected depends on the allele.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI shows variable atrophy of the cerebral cortex, brain stem, and cerebellum
evidence.explanation: Documents cerebellar atrophy in the representative ADCA-I subtype SCA17 — the macroscopic neuroimaging correlate of the Purkinje-cell and cerebellar cortical degeneration that is the convergent ADCA-I pathological endpoint.

steps/31.description: The convergent pathological endpoint across ADCA-I subtypes is progressive degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells with loss of the cerebellar cortical architecture, producing the progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and oculomotor abnormalities that define the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: SCA17 is characterized by ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, cognitive impairments, psychosis, and seizures as well as involuntary movements including chorea and dystonia
evidence.explanation: Documents the extracerebellar burden — pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, cognitive impairment, and psychiatric features — in the representative ADCA-I subtype SCA17. This combination of cerebellar plus extracerebellar involvement is exactly the feature that distinguishes the ADCA-I class from pure-cerebellar ADCA-III.

steps/32.description: The defining distinction of ADCA-I from the pure-cerebellar ADCA-III class is involvement of extracerebellar systems: brainstem and pontine nuclei, the pyramidal tracts, basal ganglia (extrapyramidal signs), peripheral sensory and motor nerves, and — in some subtypes — cognitive networks. The specific extracerebellar burden varies by subtype (e.g., motor-neuron involvement in SCA36; cognitive/psychiatric and extrapyramidal features in SCA17; peripheral neuropathy in SCA2/SCA4).

evidence.snippet: Patients exhibit usually a slowly progressive cerebellar syndrome with various combinations of oculomotor disorders, dysarthria, dysmetria/kinetic tremor, and/or ataxic gait.
evidence.explanation: The SCA clinical spectrum review documents the progressive cerebellar syndrome with ataxic gait that defines the ADCA-I parent class.

steps/33.description: Progressive gait and limb ataxia from cerebellar Purkinje-cell degeneration is the core, defining clinical feature shared by all ADCA-I subtypes. Subtype-level frequency and severity detail is deferred to the individual subtype entries (scaffold stage).

evidence.snippet: Patients exhibit usually a slowly progressive cerebellar syndrome with various combinations of oculomotor disorders, dysarthria, dysmetria/kinetic tremor, and/or ataxic gait.

evidence.snippet: They can present also with pigmentary retinopathy, extrapyramidal movement disorders (parkinsonism, dyskinesias, dystonia, chorea), pyramidal signs, cortical symptoms (seizures, cognitive impairment/behavioral symptoms), peripheral neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: SCA17 is characterized by ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, cognitive impairments, psychosis, and seizures as well as involuntary movements including chorea and dystonia

evidence.snippet: SCA17 is characterized by ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, cognitive impairments, psychosis, and seizures as well as involuntary movements including chorea and dystonia

evidence.snippet: Subclass 3 contains disorders caused by specific gene deletions, missense mutation, and nonsense mutation and includes SCA13, SCA14, SCA15/16, SCA27 and SCA28.

evidence.explanation: Supports parallel extracerebellar vulnerability in SCA3 while leaving intermediates unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Among the CAG/polyQ repeat diseases are Huntington's disease (HD) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), in which the expansions are within widely expressed proteins.

evidence.snippet: It segregated with autosomal dominant ID with non-progressive congenital cerebellar ataxia (NPCA) in two unrelated families, and was de novo deletion located in the same domain in a child presenting with NPCA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes dominant intragenic CAMTA1 rearrangements as the cause of this nonprogressive congenital ataxia.

evidence.snippet: The CAMTA1-associated phenotype was initially defined in patients with intragenic deletions and duplications who showed nonprogressive congenital ataxia, with or without intellectual disability.

The ClinGen gene-disease validity download (read 2026-09-23) classifies CAMTA1-cerebellar dysfunction with variable cognitive and behavioral abnormalities as Definitive under SOP9.

treatments/0.description: Subtype-aware supportive management addresses gait and falls, speech and swallowing, mobility and activities of daily living, nutrition, extrapyramidal manifestations, seizures, mood, cognition, and family needs. No intervention is established as disease-modifying across the entire class.

evidence.snippet: A comprehensive 24-week rehabilitation program significantly improves the motor cerebellar symptoms of spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 patients as assessed by the ataxia rating score likely as result of the partial preservation of motor learning and neural plasticity mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: Provides randomized subtype-specific support for intensive rehabilitation.

treatments/1.description: Balance, coordination, strengthening, gait, fall-prevention, and adaptive exercise programs are individualized. A 24-week randomized SCA2 study improved motor cerebellar scores, supporting rehabilitation as palliative care without implying molecular disease modification.

evidence.snippet: ADCA Type I. Further progress in molecular genetic studies will clarify future classifications

evidence.snippet: Despite linkage to chromosome 16q in 1996, the mutation causing spinocerebellar ataxia type 4 (SCA4), a late-onset sensory and cerebellar ataxia, remained unknown.

open_questions/0.rationale: ADCA-I remains clinically useful for an ataxia-plus presentation, but it is not a molecularly uniform disease. The 2011 three-subclass scheme predates resolution of SCA4 as a coding polyglycine expansion and other newer repeat discoveries. Future curation should retain the clinical umbrella while preventing obsolete subtype lists or one-branch mechanisms from becoming universal assertions.

evidence.snippet: By positional cloning, we identified a homozygous PNPT1 missense mutation (c.1424A>G predicting the protein substitution p.Glu475Gly) of a highly conserved PNPase residue within the second RNase-PH domain in a family affected by autosomal-recessive nonsyndromic hearing impairment.
evidence.explanation: The allele, its position in the protein and the phenotype it was found in.

evidence.snippet: Compound heterozygous PNPT1 variants were associated with DFNB70 causing prelingual profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vestibular dysfunction, and unilateral progressive vision loss in one family.
evidence.explanation: A second allele class - compound heterozygous rather than homozygous founder - producing the same named entity.

evidence.snippet: This missense variant was not annotated in both dbSNP and gnomAD databases. It was also absent in over 400 control individuals analyzed in the published study from Germany, Morocco and Turkey
evidence.explanation: The population-genetic argument for p.(Glu475Gly) being a disease allele rather than a rare benign variant.

evidence.snippet: The protein is essential in mice and in human cells
evidence.explanation: Why the DFNB70 alleles have to be hypomorphic rather than null: a complete absence of PNPase is not survivable. OTHER because the quoted sentence aggregates mouse knockout data and human cell-line data from several prior studies, so no single study type describes it, and BACKGROUND because it is this paper's introduction citing that earlier work rather than one of its own results.

steps/1.description:
Two PNPT1 missense alleles, inherited from unaffected carrier parents. The founding and best-characterised allele is c.1424A>G p.(Glu475Gly), which changes a highly conserved residue in the second RNase-PH domain and was found homozygous in the Moroccan family and, independently, in a Tunisian family. A South Indian family carries a different pair, p.(Ala46Gly) with p.(Asn540Ser), in compound heterozygosity.
These are hypomorphic rather than null alleles. PNPase is essential in mice and in human cells, so a complete absence of the protein is not what DFNB70 patients have; what they have is an enzyme that assembles and works badly.

evidence.snippet: In vitro analyses in bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells showed that the identified mutation results in a hypofunctional protein leading to disturbed PNPase trimerization and impaired mitochondrial RNA import.
evidence.explanation: The direct demonstration that the deafness allele breaks trimer assembly, in three heterologous systems.

evidence.snippet: We found that all pathogenic mutations tested caused defects in protein assembly and affected the degradation and RNA binding efficiency to varying degrees.
evidence.explanation: Assembly failure generalised across the PNPT1 disease alleles, including the DFNB70 allele E475G, in a single comparative study.

evidence.snippet: Structural studies on PNPases of different organisms have shown that the protein is a homotrimer in which the protomers are assembled in a doughnut shape with the KH and S1 RNA binding domains on the top of a central channel where the catalytic site is located
evidence.explanation: Why trimer assembly is the functionally decisive step rather than an incidental structural property. BACKGROUND because the sentence is the paper's summary of prior structural work, not its own result.

steps/2.description: PNPase is catalytically active only as a homotrimer, whose protomers form a doughnut with the KH and S1 RNA-binding domains above a central channel holding the catalytic site. p.(Glu475Gly) disturbs that assembly, and the 2025 survey of pathological PNPase variants found defective assembly common to every disease allele it tested. This is the step at which the two PNPase jobs downstream - RNA import and RNA degradation - both become impaired.

evidence.snippet: the Q387R and E475G variants were strongly impaired in RNA20 degradation
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of impaired degradation by the DFNB70 allele.

evidence.snippet: Human PNPase (hPNPase) is an essential RNA exonuclease located in mitochondria, where it contributes to RNA import from the cytoplasm, degradation of mitochondrial RNA and R-loop homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: The enzyme's three mitochondrial jobs, which is why an assembly defect has more than one downstream branch. BACKGROUND because it is the abstract's framing of established function rather than a finding of this work.

steps/3.description: PNPase is a 3'-5' phosphorolytic exonuclease and, with SUV3, forms the mitochondrial degradosome that clears and processes mitochondrial transcripts. The DFNB70 allele E475G was strongly impaired at degrading a model RNA substrate in vitro, alongside the COXPD13 allele Q387R. This branch is included because it is measured, not because it has been shown to be the one that deafens: the same comparative study found that catalytic impairment does not track disease severity across PNPT1 alleles.

evidence.snippet: In vitro analyses in bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells showed that the identified mutation results in a hypofunctional protein leading to disturbed PNPase trimerization and impaired mitochondrial RNA import.
evidence.explanation: The import defect attributed specifically to the deafness allele.

evidence.snippet: A subset of nuclear-encoded RNAs has to be imported into mitochondria for the proper replication and transcription of the mitochondrial genome and, hence, for proper mitochondrial function.
evidence.explanation: Why an import defect matters downstream at all. OTHER because the quoted sentence states established cell biology built from many study types rather than any one of them, and BACKGROUND because it is the paper's opening framing rather than a result of this study.

steps/4.description: A subset of nuclear-encoded RNAs has to reach the mitochondrial matrix for the organelle's genome to be replicated and transcribed, and PNPase is one of very few known components of that import route in mammals. The DFNB70 allele impairs it. How much of the hearing phenotype this branch carries, as against the degradation branch below, has not been separated experimentally.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry revealed strong PNPase staining in the murine cochlea, including the sensory hair cells and the auditory ganglion neurons.
evidence.explanation: The localisation evidence, in mouse, that places the protein in the two cell types this node names.

evidence.snippet: In summary, we show that a component of the mitochondrial RNA-import machinery is specifically required for auditory function.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion that the requirement is auditory-specific. INDIRECT because it is an inference from a human genetic result plus mouse expression, not a measurement of hair cell or ganglion neuron function in the disease state.

steps/5.description:
The site of the lesion. PNPase stains strongly in the murine cochlea, in the sensory hair cells and the auditory ganglion neurons, and the original report concludes that the mitochondrial RNA-import machinery is specifically required for auditory function. The strongest evidence that this is causal rather than correlative is a mouse in which PNPase was knocked out in inner ear hair cells and which developed progressive hearing loss, an experiment its authors relate directly to the human PNPT1 hearing phenotype.
Two gaps keep this node at PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED. That mouse carries a complete hair-cell knockout, where DFNB70 patients carry a hypomorphic allele expressed in every tissue, so it isolates the cochlear contribution without showing that the human disease is hair-cell autonomous. And the spiral ganglion arm of this node rests on expression alone: no ganglion-restricted deletion has been reported and no patient temporal bone has been examined.

evidence.snippet: Compound heterozygous PNPT1 variants were associated with DFNB70 causing prelingual profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vestibular dysfunction, and unilateral progressive vision loss in one family.
evidence.explanation: Onset, severity and sensorineural character in one sentence, attributed explicitly to DFNB70.

evidence.snippet: We describe adult siblings with biallelic PNPT1 variants identified through WES who presented with isolated severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).
evidence.explanation: A second, independently ascertained family presenting as isolated severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

steps/6.description: The defining and, in three of the four reported families, the only feature. The South Indian family's hearing loss is described as prelingual and profound; the adult siblings reported separately had severe congenital hearing loss; the Tunisian and Moroccan families are described as autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing impairment, severe in the Moroccan kindred. Bilaterality is stated for the fourth family and implied by the recessive nonsyndromic designation elsewhere.

evidence.snippet: Compound heterozygous PNPT1 variants were associated with DFNB70 causing prelingual profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vestibular dysfunction, and unilateral progressive vision loss in one family.
evidence.explanation: The only report of vestibular involvement in a DFNB70 family.

steps/7.description:
Reported in the South Indian family alongside the hearing loss. The vestibular and auditory end organs share hair cell biology and a common mitochondrial demand, so a shared lesion is the obvious reading, but no vestibular testing is reported for the other DFNB70 families and no vestibular tissue has been examined.
Read the incoming edge with that in mind. It comes from the cochlear node, and vestibular hair cells are not cochlear: no published work places PNPase in the utricle, saccule or crista, and the mouse knockout that produces hearing loss was not assessed for balance. The edge is marked INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES because it asserts a shared hair cell vulnerability and nothing more.

evidence.snippet: Even though the genetic data reported the functional importance of this residue (Glu475) suggesting the implication of this missense variation in HI, the PNPT1-ARNSHI relationship was classified as limited, when reviewed by the ClinGen Hearing Loss Working Group.
evidence.explanation: The formal gene-disease validity grading for the hearing phenotype, which is the honest summary of how much replication exists.

evidence.snippet: PNPT1 is a mitochondrial RNA transport protein that has been linked to two discrete phenotypes, namely isolated sensorineural hearing loss (OMIM 614934) and combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency (OMIM 614932).
evidence.explanation: The two recessive PNPT1 entities and the OMIM numbers that separate them, which is what makes this a separate entry from the COXPD13 one.

genes/0.notes:
The gene-disease relationship for the hearing phenotype is weakly supported and has been graded as such. The ClinGen Hearing Loss Working Group classified PNPT1 for autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing impairment as Limited, as reported in the Tunisian study; the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity download retrieved on 2026-09-25 contains exactly one PNPT1 row, PNPT1 - Leigh syndrome (MONDO:0009723), autosomal recessive, Moderate, Mitochondrial Diseases Gene Curation Expert Panel, so no separate hearing-loss assertion is currently published and none is cited here.
The same gene carries two other inherited phenotypes on different allele classes: biallelic hypomorphic missense alleles cause combined oxidative phosphorylation defect type 13 (OMIM 614932, curated separately), and heterozygous truncating and splice alleles in the S1 domain cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 25. Zygosity and allele class therefore have to be established before a PNPT1 genotype is called DFNB70.

evidence.snippet: The PNPT1-Glu475Gly variant identified in (Family.7_P7) segregated in 5 siblings born from consanguineous parents with ARNSHI
evidence.explanation: The consanguineous recessive pedigree structure that carrier testing and recurrence counselling act on.

treatments/0.description: Counselling for an autosomal recessive condition, most often in a consanguineous family: a 25 percent sibling recurrence risk once one affected child is born, carrier testing for at-risk relatives, and a discussion of the uncertain long-term neurological prognosis raised by the adult siblings reported with late multisystem disease. Counselling does not act on the mechanism; it is curated because it is the intervention the genotype itself indicates.

open_questions/0.rationale:
OMIM separates the two, 614934 and 614932, and this KB curates them as two entries. The separation has one substantial piece of evidence against it: two adult siblings diagnosed with isolated severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss developed ataxia, dystonia and cognitive decline in their forties, and optic atrophy, spasticity and incontinence thereafter. Their reporting authors ask in their title whether PNPT1-related hearing loss is ever non-syndromic, and conclude that PNPT1-related disorders may be a spectrum rather than distinct phenotypes.
Nothing settles it either way. The Moroccan and Tunisian families have not been reported in late adulthood. The South Indian family already has vestibular dysfunction and unilateral progressive vision loss alongside the deafness, so even at first report it is not quite isolated. And on the mechanistic side, the 2025 comparative study of pathological PNPase variants found that catalytic impairment does not track disease severity across PNPT1 alleles, which removes the most obvious way of predicting which phenotype an allele will give.
It matters clinically and it matters pediatrically: a child diagnosed with DFNB70 is being given a prognosis of isolated deafness on the strength of families who had not yet reached the age at which the other outcome appeared.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The tissue claim in this entry rests on immunohistochemistry: PNPase stains strongly in the murine cochlea, in the sensory hair cells and the auditory ganglion neurons, and a mouse with PNPase knocked out in inner ear hair cells develops progressive hearing loss. That establishes a requirement for the protein in hair cells; it does not establish that the DFNB70 allele acts there. The mouse is a complete knockout confined to one cell type, where patients carry a hypomorph expressed everywhere, and no mouse carrying the human deafness allele has been reported. The functional work on p.(Glu475Gly) itself was done in bacteria, yeast, mammalian cell lines and, most recently, CRISPR-edited 293T cells - none of which has a cochlea.
The harder half of the question is the tissue restriction. PNPase is essential in mice and in human cells and its loss produces multisystem disease on other alleles, so a hypomorph that deafens and does nothing else implies that the cochlea is the tissue with the lowest tolerance for reduced PNPase, or that a second factor is involved. Neither has been tested. This is filed as a human-model mismatch rather than a plain knowledge gap because the functional experiments were done - in systems whose fidelity to the cochlea is the open question.

evidence.snippet: The AGPAT2 enzyme catalyzes the acylation of lysophosphatidic acid to form phosphatidic acid, a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of triacylglycerol and glycerophospholipids.

evidence.snippet: PPARγ plays an essential role in adipogenesis, stimulating the differentiation of preadipocytes into adipocytes.
evidence.explanation: The quoted statement describes established receptor biology, not a measurement in the reviewed patients. OTHER with BACKGROUND is appropriate for this gene-level function; the same review is graded HUMAN_CLINICAL with REVIEW_SYNTHESIS when it summarizes the biallelic patient phenotype in the subtype record.

evidence.explanation: The review describes near-complete adipose tissue absence in CGL.

evidence.explanation: Supports the abnormal mitochondrion organization bound here, as distinct from the separate quantitative loss of ATP output.

evidence.snippet: The function of currently known genes suggests that PFBC could be caused by the dysfunction of the neurovascular unit, the dysregulation of phosphate homeostasis, or mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Independent review naming mitochondrial dysfunction as one of the three mechanisms of this disease, which is why it is modelled as its own node rather than folded into the phosphate-handling node.

steps/8.description: CMPK2 loss of function depletes mitochondrial DNA and mitochondrial protein in neurons and vascular endothelial cells, two brain cell types with high energy expenditure, lowering ATP production, distorting cristae architecture, and raising intracellular inorganic phosphate. This is a third initiating axis in this disease, alongside the phosphate transporters and the neurovascular-unit genes, and it converges on the same deposition step.

evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency of SLC20A2, which encodes an inorganic phosphate importer, is a major cause of autosomal-dominant PFBC.
evidence.explanation: Supports defective phosphate import as a central dominant PFBC mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These mutations alter phosphate export, implicating XPR1 and phosphate homeostasis in PFBC.
evidence.explanation: Supports defective phosphate export as a complementary PFBC mechanism.

evidence.snippet: In cells, loss of NAA60 caused reduced surface levels of SLC20A2 and a reduction in extracellular phosphate uptake.
evidence.explanation: Shows that NAA60-associated PFBC converges mechanistically on impaired SLC20A2-dependent phosphate uptake.

steps/9.description: SLC20A2 and XPR1 directly regulate inorganic phosphate influx and efflux, while NAA60 loss secondarily reduces SLC20A2 surface abundance and phosphate uptake. Together these defects dysregulate phosphate handling in the brain microvascular environment and promote calcium-phosphate deposition.

evidence.snippet: The occurrence of these calcium depositions depends on the loss of endothelial PDGF-B and correlates with the degree of pericyte and blood-brain barrier deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports neurovascular-unit failure as a cause of brain calcification.

evidence.snippet: We speculated that mutant JAM2 protein resulted in impaired cell-cell adhesion functions and reduced integrity of the neurovascular unit.
evidence.explanation: Supports tight-junction and neurovascular-unit disruption in recessive PFBC.

steps/10.description: PFBC-linked PDGFB/PDGFRB and JAM2 defects impair pericyte-endothelial-astrocyte homeostasis, while related recessive pathways such as MYORG likely converge on the same neurovascular system. Reduced blood-brain barrier maintenance and cell-cell adhesion favor vascular and perivascular brain calcification.

evidence.snippet: Primary familial brain calcification is a monogenic disease characterized by bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and other brain regions, and commonly presents motor, psychiatric, and cognitive symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Supports bilateral intracranial calcification as the core disease phenotype.

steps/11.description: Bilateral intracranial calcification involving the basal ganglia and other deep brain regions is the defining radiographic hallmark of the disorder.

edges/8.description: Dysregulated phosphate handling favors calcium-phosphate precipitation along deep-brain microvascular structures.

evidence.snippet: Notably, calcification developed in a progressive manner in the homozygous Cmpk2-KO mice thalamus region as well as in the Cmpk2-knock-in mice bearing the patient mutation, thus phenocopying the calcification pathology observed in the patients.
evidence.explanation: Connects the mitochondrial lesion to deposition: removing or mutating Cmpk2 in mouse produces the calcification itself, not only the mitochondrial phenotype.

edges/9.description: Failed mitochondrial energy metabolism with raised intracellular inorganic phosphate in high-demand neurons and vascular endothelial cells favours calcium-phosphate precipitation at the same deep-brain microvascular sites the transporter and neurovascular-unit lesions act on.

evidence.snippet: The occurrence of these calcium depositions depends on the loss of endothelial PDGF-B and correlates with the degree of pericyte and blood-brain barrier deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Supports neurovascular PDGF-B/pericyte deficiency as a driver of calcium deposition.

evidence.snippet: Primary familial brain calcification is a monogenic disease characterized by bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and other brain regions, and commonly presents motor, psychiatric, and cognitive symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Supports bilateral intracranial calcification as the clinical/radiographic manifestation of the deposition process.

edges/10.description: Calcium-phosphate deposition along neurovascular structures manifests radiographically as bilateral intracranial calcifications.

evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency of SLC20A2, which encodes an inorganic phosphate importer, is a major cause of autosomal-dominant PFBC.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SLC20A2 as the major dominant phosphate-import gene in PFBC.

evidence.snippet: These mutations alter phosphate export, implicating XPR1 and phosphate homeostasis in PFBC.
evidence.explanation: Directly links dominant XPR1 variants to PFBC through altered phosphate export.

evidence.snippet: Mutations of PDGFRB further support the involvement of this biological pathway in IBGC pathophysiology.
evidence.explanation: Supports PDGFRB as a causative dominant PFBC gene linked to the shared pathway.

evidence.snippet: Here we identify six families of different ancestry with nonsense and missense mutations in the gene encoding PDGF-B, the main ligand for PDGF-Rβ.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PDGFB as a dominant PFBC gene in affected human families.

evidence.snippet: MYORG mutations are linked to a recessive form of primary familial brain calcification.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MYORG as a recessive PFBC gene.

evidence.snippet: the MYORG protein may interact with calcium channels expressed in astrocytes
evidence.explanation: Phylogenetic-profiling analysis links MYORG to astrocyte calcium channels and to PDGFRB-interacting proteins, connecting recessive MYORG disease to the shared neurovascular PFBC pathway.

evidence.snippet: Our study identifies a novel causative gene for primary familial brain calcification, whose vital function and high expression in the neurovascular unit further supports impairment of the neurovascular unit as the root of primary familial brain calcification pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes JAM2 as a recessive PFBC gene and ties it to neurovascular pathology.

evidence.snippet: This study establishes NAA60 as a causal gene for PFBC, provides a possible biochemical explanation of its disease-causing mechanisms and underscores NAA60-mediated Nt-acetylation of transmembrane proteins as a fundamental process for healthy neurobiological functioning.
evidence.explanation: Establishes NAA60 as a recessive PFBC gene with a defined biochemical mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Here, we analyzed two brain calcification families and identified calcification co-segregated biallelic variants in the CMPK2 gene that disrupt mitochondrial functions.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CMPK2 as a recessive brain-calcification gene on co-segregation of biallelic variants in two families.

evidence.snippet: Notably, calcification developed in a progressive manner in the homozygous Cmpk2-KO mice thalamus region as well as in the Cmpk2-knock-in mice bearing the patient mutation, thus phenocopying the calcification pathology observed in the patients.
evidence.explanation: Two independent mouse models - a knockout and a knock-in carrying the patient allele - reproduce the calcification, which is what raises CMPK2 above a co-segregation observation.

evidence.snippet: Hitherto, seven genes have been associated with PFBC, including four dominant inherited genes (SLC20A2, PDGFRB, PDGFB, and XPR1) and three recessive inherited genes (MYORG, JAM2, and CMPK2).
evidence.explanation: Independent review counting CMPK2 among the established recessive PFBC genes, which is the basis for typing it CAUSATIVE rather than as a candidate.

evidence.snippet: Screening of two large cohorts of patients with unresolved brain calcifications revealed two affected French siblings and one unrelated Chinese individual, each carrying rare, biallelic, missense variants in the RRP12 gene
evidence.explanation: The replication beyond the two index Pakistani probands: three further individuals from two more families, all with biallelic missense variants.

evidence.snippet: RRP12 is a novel candidate gene for autosomal recessive brain calcifications, possibly associated with a wide clinical spectrum ranging from early-onset severe forms to adult-onset paucisymptomatic presentations.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own classification, and the reason this record is typed UNKNOWN/Candidate rather than CAUSATIVE.

evidence.snippet: Primary brain calcifications are observed in several inherited diseases due to different pathogenic mechanisms, including the disruption of the neurovascular unit, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired nucleic acid metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Names the three mechanistic axes of inherited brain calcification, which is how RRP12 is positioned relative to the other genes on this entry. Marked BACKGROUND because it is the paper's structured `BACKGROUND:` framing rather than a result of the study.

genes/8.notes: `relationship_type: UNKNOWN` with `association: Candidate` follows the founding report's own conclusion, which calls RRP12 "a novel candidate gene" rather than an established cause. Four families with biallelic variants and a protein-level readout is real support, but the two large screening cohorts it drew on (France n = 111, China n = 543) yielded three further individuals between them, its own zebrafish knockdown produced developmental delay and lethality rather than calcification, and the current ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity table (file created 2026-09-25, downloaded from the unversioned URL pinned in data/clingen/MANIFEST.yaml) contains no RRP12 assertion - nor any assertion for the other eight genes on this entry, so that silence is about the panel's coverage of this disease rather than about RRP12 specifically.

evidence.snippet: This example expands the phenotype of SLC20A2-associated PFBC patients and shows the clinical efficacy of dopaminergic replacement treatment.
evidence.explanation: Supports symptomatic dopaminergic therapy for PFBC-associated parkinsonism.

treatments/0.description: Symptomatic dopaminergic therapy can improve PFBC-associated parkinsonism, although treatment may require adjustment because motor fluctuations and dyskinesia can emerge.

evidence.snippet: Together, our findings expand the genetic etiology of PFBC and demonstrate ASO-mediated splice modulation as a potential therapy for PFBC patients with SLC20A2 haploinsufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Supports an emerging disease-modifying treatment strategy for SLC20A2-related PFBC in a preclinical model.

treatments/1.description: Experimental ASO therapy for SLC20A2 haploinsufficiency restores functional SLC20A2 expression and suppresses calcification in a humanized mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Borrelia miyamotoi, transmitted by Ixodes spp. ticks, was recognized as an agent of hard tick relapsing fever in the United States in 2013.
evidence.explanation: The human surveillance report establishes the upstream Ixodes-transmitted B. miyamotoi infection this node represents.

steps/0.description: Feeding Ixodes hard ticks deliver B. miyamotoi from a reservoir tick cycle into human skin, initiating hard-tick relapsing-fever borreliosis.

evidence.snippet: Growth inhibition assays revealed that B. miyamotoi is strongly resistant to complement-mediated bacteriolysis.
evidence.explanation: Human-serum assays show that B. miyamotoi withstands complement-mediated lysis and can therefore survive the innate serum barrier upstream of spirochetemia.

evidence.snippet: Functional analyses revealed that CbiA interacted with complement regulator Factor H (FH), C3, C3b, C4b, C5, and C9.
evidence.explanation: The CbiA functional study identifies the B. miyamotoi surface protein that binds complement regulators and effectors to inhibit human complement attack.

steps/1.description: B. miyamotoi resists human complement-mediated killing; the outer-surface protein CbiA binds Factor H and complement components, preserving Factor H cofactor activity and inhibiting complement deposition and terminal-complex assembly on the spirochete surface.

evidence.snippet: Specific laboratory diagnosis of B. miyamotoi infection is achieved through PCR detection of B. miyamotoi DNA
evidence.explanation: PCR confirmation in blood specimens establishes spirochetemia as the directly detected state in acute B. miyamotoi disease.

steps/2.description: B. miyamotoi persists as a bloodstream relapsing-fever Borrelia infection whose bacteremic burden drives fever, systemic symptoms, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated hepatic transaminases.

evidence.snippet: Our analyses revealed that the switch occurred by replacing the expression cassette and its downstream silent cassettes with the long segment from archival plasmid.
evidence.explanation: B. miyamotoi clones reisolated from experimentally infected mice directly showed Vmp long-segment conversion as the switching mechanism for expressed surface-antigen cassettes.

evidence.snippet: All relapsing fever group borreliae display antigenic variation, a shift in expressed proteins that creates recurring febrile episodes
evidence.explanation: The CDC surveillance paper explains why antigenic variation is the mechanism that makes relapsing-fever Borrelia bacteremias recur.

evidence.snippet: Relapses occurred in all the 8 patients before antibiotic treatment.
evidence.explanation: The PCR-confirmed Russian inpatient cohort documents untreated recurrent B. miyamotoi fever episodes, anchoring the recurrent-fever branch in human clinical disease.

steps/3.description: B. miyamotoi belongs to the relapsing-fever Borrelia clade whose variable major proteins mediate antigenic variation, allowing rare switched spirochete variants to escape the antibody response and drive recurrent bacteremic fever waves.

evidence.snippet: We describe a case-patient in Minnesota, USA, who had meningeal symptoms of 1 month duration. B. miyamotoi infection was diagnosed by Gram staining on cerebrospinal fluid and confirmed by sequencing.
evidence.explanation: The Minnesota case report confirms B. miyamotoi in CSF in a patient with meningeal disease.

steps/4.description: In rare severe presentations, B. miyamotoi disseminates to cerebrospinal fluid and produces meningoencephalitis, most often reported in immunocompromised hosts.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the most common symptoms were fever (89%), fatigue (75%), headache (72%), and chills (68%).
evidence.explanation: Fever was the most common symptom among 300 US surveillance cases.

steps/5.description: Fever is the dominant presenting manifestation of hard-tick relapsing fever.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the most common symptoms were fever (89%), fatigue (75%), headache (72%), and chills (68%).
evidence.explanation: Chills occurred in 68% of US surveillance cases.

steps/6.description: Chills commonly accompany B. miyamotoi fever.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the most common symptoms were fever (89%), fatigue (75%), headache (72%), and chills (68%).
evidence.explanation: Headache occurred in 72% of US surveillance cases.

steps/7.description: Headache is a common nonlocalizing symptom in B. miyamotoi disease.

evidence.snippet: A total of 28% reported recurring fevers of some kind, 55% had arthralgia, and 16% had a rash.
evidence.explanation: Arthralgia occurred in 55% of US surveillance cases.

steps/8.description: Arthralgia is frequent during the acute systemic syndrome.

evidence.snippet: A total of 28% reported recurring fevers of some kind, 55% had arthralgia, and 16% had a rash.
evidence.explanation: The CDC surveillance report documents recurring fevers among people with B. miyamotoi hard-tick relapsing fever.

steps/9.description: Borrelia miyamotoi disease can manifest with relapsing febrile episodes.

evidence.snippet: Thrombocytopenia (51/105, 49%), increased levels of aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (40/96, 42%), and leukopenia (39/105, 37%) were common laboratory abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia was present in 49% of US cases with platelet data.

steps/10.description: Thrombocytopenia is a common laboratory abnormality in acute disease.

evidence.snippet: Thrombocytopenia (51/105, 49%), increased levels of aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (40/96, 42%), and leukopenia (39/105, 37%) were common laboratory abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Leukopenia was present in 37% of US cases with leukocyte data.

steps/11.description: Leukopenia can accompany B. miyamotoi spirochetemia.

evidence.snippet: Thrombocytopenia (51/105, 49%), increased levels of aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (40/96, 42%), and leukopenia (39/105, 37%) were common laboratory abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Aminotransferases were increased in 42% of US cases with laboratory data.

steps/12.description: Aminotransferases are frequently elevated during acute disease.

evidence.snippet: Borrelia miyamotoi is an emerging tickborne pathogen that has been associated with central nervous system infections in immunocompromised patients, albeit infrequently.
evidence.explanation: The case-report abstract links B. miyamotoi to rare CNS infection in immunocompromised patients.

steps/13.description: Rare CNS B. miyamotoi infection can present with meningeal or encephalitic disease, particularly in immunocompromised hosts.

edges/0.description: Tick inoculation introduces B. miyamotoi into human tissues and blood, where the spirochete surface can block complement attack.

edges/1.description: Complement evasion lets spirochetes resist innate bacteriolysis long enough to establish bloodstream infection.

edges/2.description: The bacteremic relapsing-fever Borrelia population carries variable major-protein systems that can switch expressed surface antigens.

edges/3.description: Bacteremia manifests as acute high fever.

edges/4.description: The systemic febrile syndrome commonly includes chills.

edges/5.description: The systemic febrile syndrome commonly includes headache.

edges/6.description: The systemic febrile syndrome commonly includes joint pain.

edges/7.description: Acute infection commonly lowers the platelet count.

edges/8.description: Acute infection commonly lowers the leukocyte count.

edges/9.description: Acute infection commonly raises circulating hepatic transaminases.

edges/10.description: Rare disseminated infections reach the central nervous system, especially in immunocompromised patients.

edges/11.description: Bacteremic waves drive relapsing febrile episodes.

edges/12.description: CNS infection manifests with meningeal or encephalitic disease.

evidence.snippet: A single course of ceftriaxone or doxycycline appeared to clear B. miyamotoi infection.
evidence.explanation: The first human case series reported apparent clearance after a single ceftriaxone or doxycycline course.

evidence.snippet: Clinical isolates of B. miyamotoi are highly susceptible to doxycycline, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Clinical isolates were susceptible to doxycycline and ceftriaxone in MIC assays, supporting the same antibiotic choices mechanistically.

treatments/0.description: Antibiotic therapy clears B. miyamotoi spirochetemia and prevents further relapse; doxycycline is used for uncomplicated acute disease, and ceftriaxone has clinical and in vitro support for severe or CNS disease.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Antibiotic killing clears bloodstream B. miyamotoi.

evidence.snippet: Cigarette smoking (≥3.5 pack-years), increasing duration of employment in the textile industry and work in the spinning section were important factors found to be associated with several respiratory outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Identifies duration of employment and the specific mill section as exposure determinants, grounding the occupational specificity of this entry.

evidence.snippet: We found low inhalable dust exposures (geometric mean: 610 µg/m3).
evidence.explanation: Documents that a high symptom burden coexisted with low measured inhalable dust, which is why dust concentration alone is a poor exposure surrogate here.

evidence.snippet: A number of cohort studies have noted additive interactions between dust and smoke exposure on respiratory symptoms and lung function decline in cotton
evidence.explanation: Sources the additive dust-smoke interaction on exactly the two outcomes this entry models in its chronic arm.

evidence.snippet: Many early studies did not adequately control for smoking when evaluating respiratory outcome in textile workers, which is problematic as exposure to tobacco and organic dust may result in the same clinical symptoms or pathologic lesions.
evidence.explanation: The confounding problem that makes smoking worth an explicit record: it produces overlapping symptoms and lesions, so leaving it unmodelled would make the dust attribution look cleaner than the literature is.

evidence.snippet: In the textile industry, recognized to have high endotoxin exposure, byssinosis is an occupational respiratory disease due to exposure to cotton, hemp, or flax.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the exposure and its fibre range, and the high endotoxin content of the textile dust that the canonical model rests on.

evidence.snippet: Smoking, endotoxin, and dust concentrations were risk factors for all work-related symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Measured endotoxin and dust concentration both act as risk factors, supporting the inhaled dose of this node as the driving quantity.

steps/2.description: Mechanical opening, carding and spinning of raw cotton, flax, hemp or sisal aerosolizes respirable dust carrying gram-negative bacterial endotoxin acquired during field growth, harvest and storage, together with plant bract and trash material. Exposure is concentrated in carding and opening rooms.

evidence.snippet: The results suggest that CD14 and TLR-4 polymorphisms influence regulators of the inflammation induced by endotoxin in organic dusts.
evidence.explanation: Human genetic evidence that CD14 and TLR4 are functionally in the path between organic-dust endotoxin and the inflammatory response, which is the claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: IL-6 and ECP values were lower among those with TLR-4 /+896 AG and GG polymorphisms as compared to AA.
evidence.explanation: The specific measured effect: TLR4 genotype changes the cytokine output of endotoxin-exposed workers, tying receptor to mediator quantitatively.

steps/3.description: Inhaled endotoxin is recognized by the CD14/TLR4/MD-2 receptor complex on airway macrophages and bronchial epithelium, activating NF-kappaB-driven pro-inflammatory transcription. Human evidence for this step in byssinosis specifically is genetic rather than histological: variants in CD14 and TLR4 shift the inflammatory-mediator response to organic dust endotoxin.

evidence.snippet: Extracts of cotton mill dust (CDE) were shown to activate complement by the classical and alternative pathways.
evidence.explanation: The primary assay behind the complement activation bound on this node, establishing that cotton dust extract activates complement by both pathways.

evidence.snippet: The data presented suggest that endotoxin is not the principal complement-activating component, as complement activation could not be correlated to endotoxin concentrations of extracts of various parts of the cotton plant.
evidence.explanation: The decisive observation for this node: the complement effect does not track endotoxin content, so it is attributable to a different constituent. This is the mechanistic case for the non-endotoxin hypothesis, independent of the airway-challenge evidence below.

evidence.snippet: Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone failed to remove the complement-activating component in CDE demonstrating that polyphenolic tannins are not the causative agents.
evidence.explanation: Refutes tannin — the literature's standing candidate — as the constituent responsible for the complement branch of this node. Curated as REFUTE rather than omitted because the node's description names tannin as the usual candidate, and this is the evidence against it. The exclusion is specific to complement activation and does not rule tannin out of the bronchoconstriction branch.

evidence.snippet: a study in healthy human volunteers did not demonstrate a dose-response relationship between the endotoxin content of cotton bract extracts and acute drops in FEV1
evidence.explanation: Review statement of the dose-response failure that motivates positing a second agent at all.

evidence.snippet: endotoxin did not cause contraction of isolated tracheal smooth muscle seen with cotton dust
evidence.explanation: Isolates the specific effect endotoxin fails to reproduce — smooth-muscle contraction — which is the bronchoconstriction step this node feeds.

evidence.snippet: Endotoxin levels were low for CBE (5.71 EU/mg) and CDE (31.88 EU/mg).
evidence.explanation: Documents the low endotoxin content of the challenge material, which is half of what makes the large response below an argument for a non-endotoxin constituent.

evidence.snippet: The average maximal falls in MEF40%(P) were 70 +/- 4.9 and 70 +/- 4.4% of baseline (nonsignificant) following CBE and CDE, respectively.
evidence.explanation: The other half: a roughly 70% fall in expiratory flow from low-endotoxin extracts, in 18 and 17 of 21 healthy subjects. A large effect from little endotoxin is the case for an additional agent.

evidence.snippet: All subjects enhanced their MCh response following CBE or CDE.
evidence.explanation: Both extracts also induced airway hyperresponsiveness, so the effect is not limited to acute bronchoconstriction.

steps/4.description: A constituent of cotton dust other than endotoxin contributes to the acute airway response. Bract-derived tannin is the usual candidate, though the complement assay below excludes it for that branch specifically. Cotton bract and cotton dust extracts with low measured endotoxin provoke large falls in expiratory flow and heighten methacholine responsiveness in healthy volunteers, and cotton dust activates complement without that activation tracking endotoxin content.

evidence.snippet: The immunopathogenesis predominantly involves Toll-like receptor signaling cascade, T-helper 1/T-helper 17 lymphocyte responses, neutrophil influx
evidence.explanation: Names neutrophil influx alongside TLR signalling as the core immunopathogenesis of organic-dust airway disease, which is the step this node represents.

steps/5.description: Activated macrophages and epithelium release IL-6, IL-8 and other neutrophil chemoattractants, recruiting neutrophils into the airway lumen and bronchial mucosa and establishing a self-amplifying inflammatory response.

evidence.snippet: Histamine accumulated in the lung over the weekend is released on exposure to dust causing the symptoms of byssinosis.
evidence.explanation: States the accumulate-then-release account of the weekend-break pattern that this node models, in the paper that proposed it.

evidence.snippet: The difference in the rate of histamine metabolism relative to the rate of histamine formation in byssinotic subjects leads to a more prolonged histamine accumulation than in symptom free subjects
evidence.explanation: Proposes the host difference that would explain why only some exposed workers become byssinotic — a metabolism-versus-formation imbalance rather than a difference in exposure.

evidence.snippet: cotton and flax dusts contain agents which potentiate the formation or accumulation of histamine or both in the lungs of guinea pigs exposed to dust
evidence.explanation: The animal-model counterpart, measuring lung histamine directly rather than inferring it from blood concentrations in workers.

evidence.snippet: The results showed that the histamine levels were significantly higher in the cotton dust-exposed workers in association with significantly decreased FEV1, PEFR, and FEF25–75%, indicating bronchoconstriction of the central, larger, and peripheral airways.
evidence.explanation: Later human data pairing raised blood histamine with simultaneous obstruction across central, large and peripheral airways in exposed workers. This is the one item on this node that couples the histamine measurement to the physiological outcome in humans rather than proposing the link.

steps/6.description: Cotton and flax dust potentiate histamine formation or accumulation in the lung, possibly by recruiting mast cells and by inhibiting histamine-degrading enzyme activity. Histamine accumulated during an exposure-free interval is proposed to be released on re-exposure, which is the leading mechanistic account of why symptoms peak on the first working day after a break.

evidence.snippet: Recent endotoxin exposure was significantly associated with byssinosis, chronic bronchitis, and chronic cough.
evidence.explanation: Attaches the symptomatic and bronchitic manifestations to recent exposure, the half of the temporal split this node sits on.

steps/7.description: Sustained low-grade airway inflammation from repeated exposure drives structural change — chronic bronchitis and small-airway narrowing. This is the arm that carries the disease from a reversible daily response to a fixed deficit, and it is driven by cumulative past exposure rather than by recent exposure.

evidence.snippet: Acute airway response, measured as cross-shift change in FEV(1), to cotton dust may lead to subsequent chronic loss of lung function in exposed workers.
evidence.explanation: States the acute-to-chronic link this node's downstream edge asserts, as the hypothesis the 20-year cohort was built to test.

evidence.snippet: every 10 ml in DeltaFEV(1) drop was associated with an additional 1.5 ml/year loss in annualized FEV(1) decline
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the edge to the chronic node: a dose-response between the size of the acute drop and the rate of permanent loss.

steps/8.description: Neutrophilic inflammation, mast-cell histamine and direct smooth-muscle contraction converge on acute airway narrowing, measurable as a fall in FEV1 across a work shift or across the working week and experienced as chest tightness. Reversible in itself, and it attenuates with continued exposure — but its magnitude and frequency predict the irreversible loss below, which is why it is modelled as feeding the chronic node rather than resolving.

evidence.snippet: Cross-first-shift and cross-week falls in FEV1 reduced in magnitude during the course of the study.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of the attenuation over the first year in workers naive to cotton dust at enrolment.

evidence.snippet: a tolerance effect develops in those workers with the continued exposure
evidence.explanation: Names the phenomenon as tolerance in the authors' own words, which is what this node is called after.

steps/9.description: With continued exposure the acute cross-shift and cross-week falls shrink in magnitude — over the first working week, and further over the first year of employment. This tolerance is what produces the Monday pattern: the response is largest after a break and smaller on subsequent days. Crucially it is tolerance of the acute response only, and does not indicate that the underlying process has stopped.

evidence.snippet: Past exposure to endotoxin was associated with reduced FEV1 level among retired cotton workers.
evidence.explanation: Sources the past-exposure half of the temporal decoupling, measured in workers no longer exposed at all.

evidence.snippet: The magnitude and frequency of cross-shift drops were associated with chronic loss in FEV(1) over the entire 20-year period examined.
evidence.explanation: The 20-year result establishing that this node's deficit is predicted by the acute response, not merely coincident with the same exposure.

evidence.snippet: The mean longitudinal fall in FEV1 at 1 year was 65.5 mL (standard error = 37.2).
evidence.explanation: Measures the first-year loss in newly exposed workers, showing the chronic arm begins accruing well before the acute response has faded.

steps/10.description: Fixed, non-reversible airflow obstruction with an accelerated annual decline in FEV1 — about 10 mL/year above baseline attributable to cotton dust, plus a further increment scaled to the size of earlier acute drops. Past cumulative endotoxin exposure predicts this decline while recent exposure predicts current symptoms, so the chronic and acute phases are measurably decoupled rather than two views of one process.

evidence.snippet: Grade 1—Chest tightness and/or breathlessness on Mondays only
evidence.explanation: The original grading definition, in which work-related chest tightness on Mondays is the criterion that establishes byssinosis. OBLIGATE follows from this being the case definition rather than from a measured case series: a patient without it is not graded as having the disease.

steps/11.description: Work-related chest tightness, characteristically worst on the first working day after a break. This single symptom is the WHO case definition of byssinosis and the basis of the original Schilling grading, which makes it the defining phenotype rather than one manifestation among many.

evidence.snippet: All subjects enhanced their MCh response following CBE or CDE.
evidence.explanation: Every subject showed increased methacholine responsiveness after cotton extract challenge, which is the direct measurement of this phenotype.

steps/12.description: Heightened bronchial reactivity following cotton dust exposure, demonstrated by an increased response to methacholine challenge after inhalation of cotton dust or bract extract.

evidence.snippet: Recent endotoxin exposure was significantly associated with byssinosis, chronic bronchitis, and chronic cough.
evidence.explanation: Associates chronic bronchitis specifically with recent endotoxin exposure in the 25-year cohort.

steps/13.description: Chronic cough with sputum production in long-exposed workers, associated with recent rather than cumulative past endotoxin exposure.
