evidence.snippet: After detection of a microdeletion by array-based comparative genomic hybridization, we identified biallelic truncating mutations in the beta 1,3-galactosyltransferase-like gene (B3GALTL) in all 20 tested patients
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic truncating B3GLCT (B3GALTL) variants as the cause of Peters plus syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Our results demonstrated that PTRPLS mutations caused loss of B3GLCT enzymatic activity and/or significantly reduced protein stability.
evidence.explanation: Functional assays confirm that PTRPLS alleles are loss-of-function at the level of enzyme activity or protein stability.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our data supports the hypothesis that loss of glucose from B3GLCT substrate proteins is responsible for the defects observed in PTRPLS patients, but not for those observed in PTRPLS-like patients.
evidence.explanation: Ties the disease specifically to loss of the glucose transfer reaction and separates it from PTRPLS-like phenotypes.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in B3GLCT abolish or severely reduce beta-1,3-glucosyltransferase activity. The recurrent intronic splice-donor allele c.660+1G>A accounts for the majority of reported pathogenic alleles; frameshift, nonsense, other splice, and rare missense alleles complete the spectrum. In vitro assays show that PTRPLS-associated substitutions cause loss of catalytic activity and/or destabilize the protein, whereas substitutions found only in milder "Peters-plus-like" patients retain activity - evidence that it is specifically the loss of glucose transfer, not any B3GLCT sequence change, that produces the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, properdin from heterozygous relatives and a healthy volunteer carried the Glc-beta1,3-Fuc-Omicron-disaccharide. These data firmly establish Peters Plus syndrome as a new congenital disorder of glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Patient-versus-control comparison establishes the specific glycosylation lesion and classifies PTRPLS as a CDG.

evidence.snippet: O-fucose is added to cysteine-rich domains called thrombospondin type 1 repeats (TSRs) by protein O-fucosyltransferase 2 (POFUT2) and is elongated with glucose by β3-glucosyltransferase (B3GLCT).
evidence.explanation: States the two-enzyme sequential reaction that B3GLCT loss interrupts.

steps/2.description: POFUT2 and B3GLCT act sequentially to add an O-linked glucose-beta-1,3-fucose disaccharide to properly folded thrombospondin type-1 repeats. In PTRPLS the pathway stalls after the first step, so TSRs on target glycoproteins carry only O-fucose. This was shown directly in patient-derived properdin, the reporter protein used to establish PTRPLS as a congenital disorder of glycosylation; loss of the disaccharide on properdin remains the only human biochemical readout of functional null status.

evidence.snippet: While known ER quality-control machinery rely on identifying and tagging unfolded proteins, we find that POFUT2 and B3GLCT mediate a noncanonical ER quality-control mechanism that recognizes folded TSRs and stabilizes them by glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Defines the noncanonical, folded-state-recognizing quality-control mechanism that B3GLCT loss disrupts.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that while POFUT2 is required for secretion of all targets tested, B3GLCT only affects the secretion of a subset, consistent with the observation that B3GLCT mutant phenotypes in PPS patients are less severe than embryonic lethal phenotypes of Pofut2-null mice.
evidence.explanation: Explains the selective, sub-lethal character of the human phenotype: only some TSR targets depend on the B3GLCT step.

evidence.snippet: Forty-nine proteins are predicted to be modified by POFUT2, and nearly half are members of the ADAMTS superfamily.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the target repertoire and identifies ADAMTS proteins as the dominant substrate class.

steps/3.description: POFUT2 and B3GLCT together constitute a noncanonical endoplasmic-reticulum quality-control mechanism. Where classical ER quality control identifies and tags unfolded protein, this pathway recognizes the FOLDED TSR cotranslationally and stabilizes it by glycosylation, marking it for ER exit. Loss of the terminal glucose therefore reduces the secretion efficiency of a subset of the 49 predicted TSR-modified proteins - a subset, not all of them, which is why PTRPLS is survivable while Pofut2-null mice are embryonic lethal. Nearly half of the targets are members of the ADAMTS superfamily, which act in the extracellular matrix.

evidence.snippet: We provide strong genetic and biochemical evidence that hydrocephalus and white spotting in B3glct mutants resulted from loss of ADAMTS20, eye abnormalities from partial reduction of ADAMTS9 and cleft palate from loss of ADAMTS20 and partially reduced ADAMTS9 function.
evidence.explanation: Assigns individual PTRPLS-like malformations to specific ADAMTS effectors.

steps/4.description: Under-secretion of TSR-bearing ADAMTS metalloproteinases degrades extracellular-matrix remodelling during organogenesis. In B3glct knockout mice the pattern is target-specific: hydrocephalus and white spotting track with loss of ADAMTS20, eye abnormalities with partial reduction of ADAMTS9, and cleft palate with the combination of both.

evidence.snippet: The paracentral opacity is due to iridocorneal adhesion and the relative central clearing associated with posterior stromal thinning.
evidence.explanation: Deep phenotyping identifies the anatomical lesion underlying the corneal opacity in PTRPLS.

evidence.snippet: Peters' anomaly (PA) is a rare anterior segment dysgenesis characterized by central corneal opacity and irido-lenticulo-corneal adhesions.
evidence.explanation: Defines the anatomical lesion of Peters anomaly that this node models.

evidence.snippet: The etiology is unknown, but may involve abnormal neural crest development.
evidence.explanation: Records the pre-molecular neural-crest hypothesis for the anterior-segment lesion; it remains a plausible cellular substrate but has not been directly demonstrated for B3GLCT loss.

steps/5.description: Defective remodelling of the developing anterior eye segment produces Peters anomaly: failure to separate the lens vesicle and/or iris from the surface ectoderm-derived cornea, leaving posterior corneal (Descemet membrane and endothelium) defects with iridocorneal and sometimes keratolenticular adhesions. Deep ocular phenotyping in PTRPLS most often shows an avascular paracentral ring opacity caused by iridocorneal adhesion, with relative central clearing over an area of posterior stromal thinning; a large vascularized central opacity is the less common alternative pattern. Periocular neural-crest-derived mesenchyme populates these structures, and abnormal neural crest development was the leading pre-molecular hypothesis for the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: short stature with rhizomelic shortening of the limbs
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the rhizomelic pattern of limb shortening.

steps/15.description: Proximal (humerus/femur) predominant limb shortening, giving the disproportion its rhizomelic character.

evidence.snippet: Peters anomaly of the eye (anterior segment dysgenesis), disproportionate short stature, brachydactyly, dysmorphic facial features, developmental delay
evidence.explanation: Lists brachydactyly among the core clinical features of PTRPLS. Classified OTHER because the quoted sentence is this in vitro study's restatement of the established human clinical description rather than new patient data.

evidence.snippet: characterized by defects in eye development, prominent forehead, hypertelorism, short stature and brachydactyly
evidence.explanation: Independent listing of brachydactyly in the clinical definition. Classified OTHER because the quoted sentence is this mouse study's restatement of the established human clinical description, not data from the mouse model or from patients it studied.

steps/16.description: Short digits, part of the characteristic hand and foot morphology.

evidence.snippet: rhizomelic shortening of the limbs with broad hands and feet
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents broad hands as part of the skeletal phenotype.

steps/17.description: Broad palms accompanying the brachydactyly; together with broad feet this is a recognizable part of the syndrome gestalt.

evidence.snippet: rhizomelic shortening of the limbs with broad hands and feet
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents broad feet as part of the skeletal phenotype.

steps/18.description: Broad feet, the pedal counterpart of the broad hands.

evidence.snippet: Major symptoms are extremely variable anterior chamber anomalies, cupid bow of the upper lip, cleft lip and palate, short stature, broad hands and feet, and variable mental delay.
evidence.explanation: Clinical review lists the cupid's-bow upper lip among the major manifestations.

steps/19.description: A distinctive upper-lip vermilion contour ("cupid's bow"), one of the most recognizable facial features of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: characterized by defects in eye development, prominent forehead, hypertelorism, short stature and brachydactyly
evidence.explanation: Prominent forehead listed among the defining clinical features. Classified OTHER because the quoted sentence is this mouse study's restatement of the established human clinical description rather than its own patient or model data.

steps/20.description: Broad, prominent forehead contributing to the characteristic facies.

evidence.snippet: characterized by defects in eye development, prominent forehead, hypertelorism, short stature and brachydactyly
evidence.explanation: Hypertelorism listed among the defining clinical features. Classified OTHER because the quoted sentence is this mouse study's restatement of the established human clinical description rather than its own patient or model data.

steps/21.description: Increased interorbital distance, part of the facial gestalt.

evidence.snippet: and, occasionally, cleft lip/palate and congenital heart defects
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes cleft lip/palate as an occasional finding, which maps to the OCCASIONAL frequency band (5-29%) in the project's prose-to-enum mapping table.

steps/22.description: Cleft of the upper lip, occurring in a subset of affected individuals and often together with cleft palate.

evidence.snippet: and, occasionally, cleft lip/palate and congenital heart defects
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes cleft lip/palate as an occasional finding, which maps to the OCCASIONAL frequency band (5-29%) in the project's prose-to-enum mapping table.

steps/23.description: Cleft of the secondary palate, occurring in a subset of affected individuals; mechanistically attributed in the mouse model to combined ADAMTS20 loss and ADAMTS9 reduction.

evidence.snippet: In properdin from patients, we could not detect the Glc-beta1,3-Fuc-Omicron-disaccharide, and we only found Fuc-Omicron-at all four Omicron-fucosylation sites.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration in patient material that the disaccharide is absent and only the O-fucose monosaccharide remains.

edges/1.description: Without B3GLCT activity the O-fucose added to TSRs by POFUT2 cannot be elongated to the Glc-beta1,3-Fuc disaccharide.

evidence.snippet: In vitro unfolding assays demonstrate that fucose and glucose stabilize folded TSRs in an additive manner.
evidence.explanation: Direct biophysical evidence that the terminal glucose contributes to TSR stability, which is the immediate consequence of B3GLCT loss.

edges/2.description: Fucose and glucose stabilize the folded TSR additively; without the glucose, folded TSRs are less stable and ER exit is less efficient.

evidence.snippet: Combined, these results provide compelling evidence that ADAMTS9 and ADAMTS20 were differentially sensitive to B3GLCT inactivation and suggest that the developmental defects in PTRPLS result from disruption of a subset of highly sensitive POFUT2/B3GLCT targets such as ADAMTS20.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ADAMTS9/ADAMTS20 as the key effectors downstream of B3GLCT loss in the mouse model.

edges/3.description: ADAMTS9 and ADAMTS20 are among the TSR targets most sensitive to loss of the disaccharide, and mouse genetics attributes distinct PTRPLS-like defects to each.

evidence.snippet: eye abnormalities from partial reduction of ADAMTS9
evidence.explanation: Attributes the ocular arm of the phenotype to partial ADAMTS9 loss.

edges/4.description: Reduced ADAMTS9 activity is the mouse-genetic correlate of the ocular defects; the intervening steps between reduced ADAMTS9 secretion and failure of anterior-segment separation are not established.

evidence.snippet: The mouse B3glct mutants developed craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities comparable to PTRPLS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that loss of B3GLCT is sufficient to produce the craniofacial and skeletal phenotype in vivo.

edges/5.description: B3glct knockout mice reproduce the craniofacial and skeletal arm of the human phenotype, but the specific TSR targets mediating growth-plate and craniofacial effects have not been resolved.

evidence.snippet: cleft palate from loss of ADAMTS20 and partially reduced ADAMTS9 function
evidence.explanation: Assigns the orofacial-clefting arm to a two-target ADAMTS deficit.

edges/6.description: Cleft palate in the mouse model requires combined ADAMTS20 loss and partial ADAMTS9 reduction.

evidence.snippet: We provide strong genetic and biochemical evidence that hydrocephalus and white spotting in B3glct mutants resulted from loss of ADAMTS20, eye abnormalities from partial reduction of ADAMTS9 and cleft palate from loss of ADAMTS20 and partially reduced ADAMTS9 function.
evidence.explanation: Mouse genetic dissection attributing hydrocephalus to the ADAMTS20 arm of the pathway; the human counterpart is the postmortem fetal finding cited on the phenotype itself.

edges/7.description: In the B3glct knockout mouse, hydrocephalus is attributed to loss of ADAMTS20; hydrocephalus is also documented in human PTRPLS fetuses at postmortem, so this is a shared severe/prenatal manifestation. The intermediate steps between ADAMTS20 loss and ventricular enlargement are not established.

evidence.snippet: Peters Plus syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by anterior eye chamber defects, disproportionate short stature, developmental delay, and cleft lip and/or palate.
evidence.explanation: Supports cleft lip as a manifestation of the monogenic syndrome and hence downstream of the ADAMTS-mediated matrix deficit; marked INDIRECT because it evidences the association, not the specific mechanistic route.

edges/8.description: Cleft lip reflects failure of the upper-lip/primary-palate fusion events, which are developmentally adjacent to but distinct from secondary palatal shelf fusion; lip clefting is part of the human syndrome definition, but the mouse dissection addressed only the secondary palate, so the specific TSR targets mediating lip involvement are not established.

evidence.snippet: Peters' anomaly (PA) is a rare anterior segment dysgenesis characterized by central corneal opacity and irido-lenticulo-corneal adhesions.
evidence.explanation: States that Peters anomaly is the clinical expression of anterior segment dysgenesis, which is the causal claim this edge makes.

edges/9.description: The specific arrest pattern - failure of the lens vesicle and iris to separate cleanly from the developing cornea, leaving a posterior corneal defect with iridocorneal and sometimes keratolenticular adhesion - is what defines Peters anomaly, the cardinal ocular malformation of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The paracentral opacity is due to iridocorneal adhesion and the relative central clearing associated with posterior stromal thinning.
evidence.explanation: Deep ocular phenotyping attributes the opacity directly to the iridocorneal adhesion produced by the dysgenesis.

edges/10.description: The posterior corneal defect and iridocorneal adhesion render the cornea opaque; in PTRPLS the typical result is an avascular paracentral ring opacity with relative central clearing.

evidence.snippet: Peters eye anomaly is a fusion of the cornea and lens due to persistence of the embryonic lens stalk
evidence.explanation: States the embryological basis of the lens involvement. Classified OTHER because the sentence is this mouse study's restatement of established human embryology rather than its own data.

edges/11.description: Failure of the lens vesicle to separate from the surface ectoderm leaves keratolenticular adhesion and predisposes to cataract.

edges/12.description: Dysgenesis of the iridocorneal angle and aqueous outflow structures - modeled at module level as a maldeveloped outflow pathway - impairs aqueous drainage and raises intraocular pressure; GeneReviews accordingly records an increased glaucoma risk requiring lifelong surveillance.

evidence.snippet: it results in corneal opacity, with severe visual impairment and other eye complications
evidence.explanation: Ties visual impairment to the corneal opacity produced by the anomaly. Classified OTHER because the sentence is this mouse study's restatement of the established human clinical picture rather than its own data.

edges/13.description: Vision is lost through the known intermediates of the dysgenesis: corneal opacity occluding the visual axis, its complications, and deprivation amblyopia when the axis is not cleared early.

edges/14.description: Impaired endochondral growth, weighted toward the proximal long bones, produces the disproportionate short stature that is one of the three defining clinical axes; the node's cited human and mouse evidence covers this summary edge.

edges/15.description: The proximal (humerus/femur) predominance of the growth deficit gives the limb shortening its rhizomelic pattern.

edges/16.description: The same endochondral growth deficit shortens the tubular bones of the digits.

edges/17.description: Altered hand skeletal proportions accompany the brachydactyly, producing the broad palms of the syndrome gestalt.

edges/18.description: The pedal counterpart of the broad hands, from the same altered skeletal proportions.

edges/19.description: Disturbed craniofacial skeletal growth shapes the calvarium; B3glct knockout mice reproduce comparable craniofacial abnormalities.

edges/20.description: Increased interorbital distance is a craniofacial skeletal proportion defect of the same growth disturbance.

edges/21.description: The distinctive upper-lip vermilion contour is part of the characteristic facies produced by disturbed craniofacial development, but the specific developmental steps shaping this soft-tissue feature have not been resolved.

edges/22.description: Failure of the palatal shelves to elevate and fuse leaves a cleft of the secondary palate; the node's cited mouse genetics attributes this to combined ADAMTS20 loss and partial ADAMTS9 reduction.

evidence.snippet: we identified biallelic truncating mutations in the beta 1,3-galactosyltransferase-like gene (B3GALTL) in all 20 tested patients
evidence.explanation: Establishes B3GLCT (B3GALTL) as the single causal gene.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with previous reports, the c.660+1G>A mutation was the most common mutation identified, seen in eight of the nine patients and accounting for 55% of pathogenic alleles in this study and 69% of all reported pathogenic alleles
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the dominance of the recurrent c.660+1G>A splice allele in the mutation spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in B3GALTL were identified in all four patients with typical Peters Plus syndrome, while no mutations were found in the remaining four patients that demonstrated some but not all characteristic features of the syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Shows that B3GLCT variants segregate with the complete syndrome and not with partial phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: either biallelic pathogenic variants in B3GLCT or compound heterozygosity for one pathogenic variant in B3GLCT and a contiguous gene deletion of 13q12.3 that includes B3GLCT
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews defines the two molecular genotype configurations that establish the diagnosis, including the contiguous-deletion allele.

evidence.snippet: Unsurprisingly, B3GLCT and PAX6 were the most frequently implicated genes, respectively in syndromic and isolated PA.
evidence.explanation: In the largest Peters anomaly cohort reported, B3GLCT is the leading gene for the syndromic form specifically, while PAX6 leads for isolated Peters anomaly.

genes/0.notes: B3GLCT (13q12.3, formerly B3GALTL) encodes beta-1,3-glucosyltransferase. Biallelic loss-of-function variants, or one loss-of-function variant in trans with a contiguous 13q12.3 deletion including B3GLCT, cause PTRPLS. The recurrent splice-donor variant c.660+1G>A is by far the most common pathogenic allele; frameshift, nonsense, other splice, and rare activity-abolishing missense alleles account for the remainder. Because a contiguous-deletion allele is part of the mutational spectrum, copy-number analysis should accompany sequencing. B3GLCT variants are characteristically absent in isolated Peters anomaly and in partial "Peters-plus-like" phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including ophthalmology to manage eye anomalies; low vision services as needed; orthopedics, physical therapy, and occupational therapy to determine need for adaptive devices to address mobility and fine motor needs; educational support for developmental delay and/or intellectual disability; cleft lip/palate team; social services to develop a plan for transition from pediatric care to adult care.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendation defining the supportive-care model.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy - no B3GLCT replacement, substrate, chaperone, gene, or RNA therapy exists. Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, coordinating ophthalmology, orthopedics, rehabilitation therapies, educational support, a cleft lip/palate team, and social services including planning the transition from pediatric to adult care.

evidence.snippet: Multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including ophthalmology to manage eye anomalies; low vision services as needed
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews assigns management of the eye anomalies to ophthalmology, with low-vision services as adjunct.

treatments/1.description: Surgical management of the anterior-segment anomaly, which may include penetrating keratoplasty or keratoprosthesis for visually significant opacity, lensectomy, and glaucoma procedures. Decisions are individualized: severe bilateral dysgenesis, glaucoma, graft failure, and retinal complications can limit the benefit, and surgery is sometimes deliberately deferred.

evidence.snippet: monitor emergence of new ophthalmologic manifestations including glaucoma in early infancy, then at age three months and age six months, and a minimum of every six months thereafter
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance schedule for glaucoma.

treatments/2.description: Because glaucoma can develop at any age and threatens residual vision, GeneReviews recommends intraocular-pressure and ophthalmologic surveillance in early infancy, again at three and six months of age, and at least every six months thereafter. Early infancy is also the critical window for detecting and treating deprivation amblyopia.

evidence.snippet: orthopedics, physical therapy, and occupational therapy to determine need for adaptive devices to address mobility and fine motor needs
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommendation for rehabilitation therapy.

treatments/3.description: Physical and occupational therapy, coordinated with orthopedics, to address mobility and fine-motor needs arising from short stature, rhizomelia, and hand anomalies, and to determine the need for adaptive devices.

evidence.snippet: cleft lip/palate team
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews assigns cleft management to a dedicated multidisciplinary team.

treatments/4.description: Surgical repair and longitudinal management of cleft lip and/or palate by a dedicated cleft team, when clefting is present, together with feeding, speech, dental, and audiology support.

evidence.snippet: Monitor the individual's response to supportive care (including educational, neurobehavioral, and musculoskeletal needs)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation covering the developmental and educational domain.

treatments/5.description: Individualized educational support and early-intervention services for developmental delay and/or intellectual disability, with monitoring of educational, neurobehavioral, and musculoskeletal needs over time.

evidence.snippet: Once the pathogenic variants involving B3GLCT have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing for PTRPLS are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic-counseling recommendation.

treatments/6.description: Counseling on autosomal recessive recurrence risk. Once the familial B3GLCT variants are known, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing are available. Counseling should note that the observed sibling risk at birth is below the theoretical 25% because of increased fetal loss.

evidence.snippet: The presented data show that both sequence and function of B3GLCT/b3glct genes is conserved in vertebrates. At the same time, complete b3glct deficiency in zebrafish appears to be inconsequential and possibly compensated for by a yet unknown mechanism.
evidence.explanation: States the mismatch and the compensation hypothesis explicitly.

evidence.snippet: The mouse B3glct mutants developed craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities comparable to PTRPLS.
evidence.explanation: Contrasting mouse result that makes the zebrafish outcome a genuine cross-species discrepancy rather than a general model limitation.

open_questions/0.rationale: Zebrafish b3glcta/b3glctb double nulls have no detectable enzyme activity yet develop normally, while B3glct knockout mice reproduce much of the human syndrome and human biallelic loss is severe. The mismatch is not a failure of gene conservation - the zebrafish enzymes are catalytically equivalent to human B3GLCT - so it points to a species-specific compensatory route for TSR folding, or to a difference in the dosage sensitivity of the ADAMTS targets. Identifying that compensation would name a candidate therapeutic bypass of the human defect, so this is a mechanistically loaded rather than incidental discrepancy. It also means negative zebrafish results must not be treated as evidence against a proposed PTRPLS mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Previous studies suggested that O-linked fucose is essential for folding and secretion of POFUT2-modified proteins and that B3GLCT-mediated extension to the disaccharide is essential for only a subset of targets.
evidence.explanation: States the selective-dependency problem that this gap addresses.

evidence.snippet: Although 49 putative targets are known, the function of the disaccharide and its role in PPS remain unexplored.
evidence.explanation: Frames the size of the target repertoire against which per-phenotype attribution is still missing.

open_questions/1.rationale: Mouse genetics implicates ADAMTS20 and ADAMTS9 for hydrocephalus, white spotting, cleft palate, and eye defects, but the human phenotype includes features not explained by these two targets (rhizomelic short stature, brachydactyly, the characteristic facies, congenital heart and renal defects). The phenotypes this gap attaches to are the ones deliberately left without a causal edge in this entry: no specific TSR target has been tied to the cardiac, renal, posterior-segment ocular (microphthalmia, coloboma), midline CNS (corpus callosum, Dandy-Walker), or cognitive manifestations, and wiring them to the generic ADAMTS node would assert an attribution the literature has not made. The correspondence is not uniform in the other direction either: hydrocephalus, initially conspicuous as a mouse finding, is in fact documented in human PTRPLS fetuses at postmortem, so it appears to be a genuinely shared severe/prenatal feature that liveborn clinical series under-report - whereas white coat spotting has no human counterpart at all. Systematic mapping of which targets are under-secreted in patient cells and which tissues depend on each would turn the pathway model into a per-phenotype mechanism, and would clarify which apparent species differences are real versus ascertainment artifacts.

evidence.snippet: We have established a sensitive immunopurification-mass spectrometry method, using multiple reaction monitoring, to analyze Omicron-fucosyl glycans.
evidence.explanation: Describes the research assay that would need to be translated into a clinical test.

open_questions/2.rationale: Unlike the N-glycosylation CDGs, PTRPLS has no routine screening assay - serum transferrin isoelectric focusing is normal - so diagnosis is entirely genotype-driven. The properdin glycoform assay is a validated research-grade biochemical readout of functional null status in patient material, but it has not been converted into an available clinical test. Without one there is no way to assay the functional consequence of a B3GLCT variant of uncertain significance, and no pharmacodynamic endpoint for a future therapy.

steps/0.description: Abnormal growth of germinal center B-cells with mutations in BCL2 and EZH2, affecting apoptosis regulation and epigenetic control.

steps/1.description: Chronic active B-cell receptor signaling with downstream NF-κB activation due to CD79B and MYD88 mutations.

steps/2.description: IRF4 rearrangement drives transcriptional programs at germinal center exit and plasmacytic differentiation, enriched in Waldeyer's ring.

steps/3.description: MYC-driven transcriptional acceleration with BCL2 and/or BCL6 anti-apoptotic co-drivers, aggressive clinical behavior.

steps/4.description: Epstein-Barr virus latency programs (LMP1, EBNA) drive B-cell proliferation and immune evasion in tonsillar B-cells.

evidence.snippet: We report six cases of primary tonsillar lymphoma with a median patient age of 42 years. There were two lymphoma cases with diffuse large cells, two cases with mixed small and large cells, one with small cells and one indeterminate. They were treated with six cycles of chemotherapy and cervical radiotherapy. All patients achieved durable complete remission.
evidence.explanation: This case series of primary tonsillar lymphoma treated all patients with six cycles of chemotherapy (with radiotherapy) and achieved durable complete remission, supporting systemic chemotherapy as an effective treatment; the specific regimen is not named in the abstract.

evidence.snippet: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) with or without rituximab (R-CHOP)... Chemotherapy treatment plans differ between the main subtypes of lymphoma.
evidence.explanation: The study mentions the use of CHOP regimen for treating non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which includes primary tonsillar lymphoma.

treatments/0.description: Systemic treatment aimed at eradicating lymphoma cells, often using CHOP regimen (Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Prednisone).

evidence.snippet: RT significantly improved overall survival in both univariate (P < 0.001) and multivariate (P = 0.002) analyses.
evidence.explanation: In the largest population-based series of primary tonsil diffuse large B cell lymphoma to date, radiation therapy was associated with significantly improved overall survival, directly supporting radiation therapy as a treatment for this disease.

evidence.snippet: From this limited series, radiotherapy alone would appear to be sufficient initial therapy for Stage IE patients, whereas Stage IIE patients probably benefit from the addition of prophylactic chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: This 65-case clinicopathologic series of primary tonsillar lymphoma concludes that radiotherapy alone can be sufficient initial therapy for localized (Stage IE) disease, supporting radiation to the tonsil for local disease control.

evidence.snippet: There have been many reports that favor aggressive systemic treatment with chemotherapy and radiotherapy, even for well-localized lymphomas, avoiding the need for tonsillectomy of the normal tonsil.
evidence.explanation: This case series of primary tonsillar lymphoma treated all six patients with chemotherapy plus cervical radiotherapy, reflecting the use of radiotherapy as part of standard management of localized disease.

treatments/1.description: Targeted radiation to the tonsil and surrounding structures to control local disease.

evidence.snippet: Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody directed against the B cell-specific protein CD20, has revolutionized lymphoma treatment by providing a highly effective form of therapy with relatively mild toxic side effects.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the use of rituximab as a targeted therapy for B-cell lymphomas.

evidence.snippet: We report six cases of primary tonsillar lymphoma with a median patient age of 42 years. ... They were treated with six cycles of chemotherapy and cervical radiotherapy.
evidence.explanation: This reference discusses chemotherapy and radiotherapy for primary tonsillar lymphoma but does not mention rituximab.

evidence.snippet: Iodine 131-tositumomab and ibritumomab tiuxetan, radioimmunoconjugates that target the CD20 antigen, have been approved in the United States for use in relapsed or refractory, indolent, and transformed B-cell lymphomas.
evidence.explanation: This reference documents approved CD20-targeted radioimmunoconjugates (tositumomab and ibritumomab tiuxetan) for B-cell lymphomas, supporting CD20-directed targeted therapy as a treatment class for B-cell lymphoma; it does not itself discuss rituximab.

evidence.snippet: While the innovations in terms of B-cell lymphomas are certainly less significant, mention must also be made of the value of rituximab combined with polychemotherapy (CHOP) and of lenalidomide (as second-line therapy) in primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type.
evidence.explanation: This reference mentions rituximab as part of the treatment for a specific type of B-cell lymphoma, but not specifically for primary tonsillar lymphoma.

evidence.snippet: The addition of rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, to upfront therapy has improved survival outcomes for high-risk patients and may allow decreased total chemotherapy in those with low-risk disease.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the use of rituximab as a targeted therapy for B-cell lymphomas.

treatments/2.description: Use of drugs like rituximab for B-cell lymphomas.

evidence.snippet: Results of conventional or high-dose chemotherapy for peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) are unsatisfactory, leaving a potential role for autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation.
evidence.explanation: This review concerns peripheral T-cell lymphoma in general rather than tonsillar lymphoma specifically; it partially supports the claim by showing that stem cell transplantation is considered for lymphoma subtypes (including the T-cell histologies that can present in the tonsil) when chemotherapy results are unsatisfactory.

treatments/3.description: Considered in certain cases where high-dose chemotherapy is followed by infusion of healthy stem cells to restore bone marrow function.

evidence.snippet: The novel mutation c.3670G>A in exon 21, inherited from the father, is likely to impair insulin receptor function by disrupting tyrosine kinase activity
evidence.explanation: A worked variant example impairing insulin-receptor tyrosine-kinase function.

evidence.snippet: The mutation also caused a reduction in the affinity of the receptor to insulin
evidence.explanation: Describes reduced receptor-insulin affinity as a consequence of INSR mutation.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in the insulin receptor gene (INSR, 19p13.2) reduce the number and/or function of cell-surface insulin receptors, most commonly through missense substitutions that impair receptor processing, insulin-binding affinity, or tyrosine-kinase activity. This is the initiating molecular lesion of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Insulin resistance is defined as the inability of target tissues to mount a normal coordinated glucose-lowering response at a normal plasma insulin level
evidence.explanation: Defines the impaired target-tissue insulin response that this node represents.

steps/2.description: Loss of functional insulin receptor blunts the downstream insulin receptor signalling pathway, principally the PI3K-AKT metabolic arm, in liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue, so target tissues fail to mount a normal glucose-lowering response to insulin.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium data were available from 10 patients and revealed hypercalciuria in all
evidence.explanation: Documents universal hypercalciuria underlying the nephrocalcinosis.

evidence.snippet: Renal tubular dysfunction with nephrocalcinosis is almost invariably present
evidence.explanation: Independent series confirming near-invariable renal tubular dysfunction with nephrocalcinosis.

steps/3.description: The insulin receptor is expressed throughout the nephron. Biallelic INSR loss produces hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis that appear tissue-autonomous (present with normotension and stable glomerular function), rather than being a secondary complication of hyperglycaemia.

evidence.snippet: Donohue syndrome (DS) and Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome (RMS) are extreme forms of insulin resistance (IR) caused by biallelic mutations in the insulin receptor gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes extreme insulin resistance as the defining state of the syndrome.

steps/4.description: Extreme, generalized insulin resistance is the cardinal systemic consequence, driving compensatory hyperinsulinaemia and the early paradoxical glycaemic pattern.

evidence.snippet: At birth, patients with RMS also show fasting hypoglycemia due to severely increased insulin levels, but with progression of the disease, insulin levels decline
evidence.explanation: Documents the early paradoxical hypoglycaemia and its later decline.

evidence.snippet: At an early stage, fasting hypoglycemia with postprandial hyperglycemia and significant hyperinsulinemia with subsequent development of insulin-resistant diabetes is observed.
evidence.explanation: Directly describes the paradoxical fasting-hypoglycaemia/postprandial-hyperglycaemia pattern.

steps/5.description: In infancy and early childhood, severely elevated insulin acting on residual receptor and cross-reactive pathways produces fasting hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperglycaemia; with disease progression insulin levels decline and sustained hyperglycaemia supervenes.

evidence.snippet: Hyperinsulinemia is typically observed early in the lives of RMS patients
evidence.explanation: Establishes early compensatory hyperinsulinaemia in RMS.

evidence.snippet: the mean fasting insulin was 349.96 μIU/mL, and the average fasting C-peptide was 6.00 ng/mL.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the extreme fasting hyperinsulinaemia and C-peptide in the pooled cohort.

steps/6.description: Pancreatic beta-cell hypersecretion produces the extreme hyperinsulinaemia that is the earliest biochemical hallmark of the syndrome (median fasting insulin ~300 uIU/mL, versus a normal range of 5-20 uIU/mL). Chronic hyperinsulinaemia cross-activates IGF-1 receptors in skin and ovary and ultimately exhausts beta-cell reserve.

evidence.snippet: High levels of insulin stimulate IGF receptors, thereby promoting the proliferation of keratinocytes.
evidence.explanation: States the IGF-receptor cross-activation mechanism driving keratinocyte proliferation.

steps/7.description: Chronic supraphysiologic insulin cross-activates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts, promoting epidermal proliferation that manifests as acanthosis nigricans and contributes to soft-tissue overgrowth.

evidence.snippet: Girls are diagnosed with hyperandrogenism, ovarian enlargement and clitoral hypertrophy.
evidence.explanation: Documents the ovarian hyperandrogenism phenotype; the theca-cell mechanism is inferred.

steps/8.description: In females, extreme hyperinsulinaemia acting on ovarian theca cells drives androgen biosynthesis, producing hyperandrogenism, enlarged/polycystic ovaries, and clitoromegaly.

evidence.snippet: The severe insulin resistance leads to hyperinsulinism with pancreatic β-cell decompensation, diabetes, hyperglycemia and ultimately ketoacidosis
evidence.explanation: Directly links beta-cell decompensation to diabetes and ketoacidosis.

steps/9.description: Sustained compensatory hypersecretion eventually exhausts beta-cell reserve, so hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia gives way to sustained hyperglycaemia and overt insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus.

evidence.snippet: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome (RMS) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the insulin receptor gene (INSR) leading to insulin-resistant diabetes, microvascular complications, and growth hormone resistance with short stature.
evidence.explanation: Names growth hormone resistance with short stature as a defining feature.

evidence.snippet: Basal growth hormone (GH) was increased (7.9 μg/L)with normal insuline-like growth factor 1 (37.6 nmol/L) suggestive of GH resistance.
evidence.explanation: A case with elevated basal GH and normal IGF-1 interpreted as GH resistance.

steps/10.description: Affected individuals show a growth-hormone-resistant state (elevated basal GH with low-normal IGF-1) and severe growth retardation that is not corrected by exogenous growth hormone or standard-dose IGF-1.

evidence.snippet: Acanthosis was present in 29 cases (29/42, 69.05%); growth retardation in 25 cases (25/42, 59.52%); dental anomalies including absence of teeth, crowding, and malocclusion in 23 cases (23/42, 54.76%); and hirsutism in 17 cases (17/42, 40.48%).
evidence.explanation: Reports acanthosis nigricans in 29/42 pooled patients.

steps/11.description: Velvety hyperpigmented skin thickening at the neck, axillae, and groin; the most frequent dermatologic sign, present in about 69% of pooled cases.

evidence.snippet: growth retardation in 25 cases (25/42, 59.52%)
evidence.explanation: Reports growth retardation in 25/42 pooled patients.

steps/12.description: Prenatal and postnatal growth failure with short stature, present in about 60% of pooled cases and often refractory to growth hormone.

evidence.snippet: large genitalia (8/42, 19.05%), hypertrophy of nails (6/42, 14.29%)
evidence.explanation: Reports large genitalia in 8/42 pooled patients.

steps/13.description: Enlarged external genitalia, including clitoromegaly in females; present in about 19% of pooled cases and related to hyperinsulinaemia-driven androgen excess.

evidence.snippet: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome (RMS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR), leading to severe insulin resistance.

evidence.snippet: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome (RMS) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the insulin receptor gene (INSR) leading to insulin-resistant diabetes, microvascular complications, and growth hormone resistance with short stature.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) INSR variants are necessary and sufficient; the functional consequence is loss/partial loss of function (captured as functional_impact_category on the Biallelic INSR Loss-of-Function pathophysiology node). In the largest pooled series (55 distinct variants across 42 patients), missense substitutions predominated (72.7%), with deletions (10.9%), insertions (1.8%), and nonsense (1.8%) variants also observed; the most recurrent variant was p.Glu238Lys and exon 2 was most frequently affected. No genotype-phenotype correlation was established. RMS occupies a hypomorphic position relative to Donohue syndrome (near-complete loss of receptor function).

treatments/1.description: When hyperglycaemia persists, high-dose insulin is used, especially during diabetic ketoacidosis, though extreme insulin resistance limits its efficacy.

evidence.snippet: After 10 months of treatment, empagliflozin therapy led to a clinically meaningful reduction in HbA1c levels, decreasing from 8.5% to 7.1%, along with an improvement in TIR from 47% to 74%.
evidence.explanation: Documents HbA1c and time-in-range improvement with empagliflozin in an RMS case.

evidence.snippet: eleven months after implementation of empagliflozin, the patient was diagnosed with an early form of nephrocalcinosis.

treatments/2.description: Empagliflozin, added off-label, lowers glucose via insulin-independent renal glucose excretion and improved HbA1c and time-in-range in a reported case; it carries a possible risk of promoting nephrocalcinosis.

evidence.snippet: Sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are a potentially interesting therapy option for people with severe genetic insulin resistance due to their ability to reduce glycemia through a mechanism that is independent of insulin action.
evidence.explanation: Explains the insulin-independent mechanism relevant to receptoropathy.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: SGLT2 inhibition lowers glucose independently of insulin action.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic benefits of rhIGF-1 included improved glycemic control and fasting tolerance in early years of life, and some growth enhancement.

evidence.snippet: Current treatment options remain unsatisfactory as high-dose rhIGF-1 exerts only limited beneficial effects and does not prevent decompensation to diabetes mellitus.

treatments/3.description: Recombinant human IGF-1 signals through the IGF-1 receptor, partially bypassing the defective insulin receptor. It improves glycaemic control and fasting tolerance in early life with some growth enhancement, but benefits are limited and it does not prevent decompensation to diabetes; continuous subcutaneous infusion may outperform bolus injection.

evidence.snippet: continuous subcutaneous rhIGF-I infusion via an insulin pump improved weight development and diabetes control (HbA1c decreased from 10 to 7.6%)
evidence.explanation: Documents metabolic improvement with continuous rhIGF-1, bypassing the defective receptor.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: IGF-1 activates partially shared post-receptor pathways, bypassing INSR.

evidence.snippet: Over time, metreleptin-treated subjects maintained 1.8 percentage point lower A1c vs controls (P = 0.007)
evidence.explanation: Controlled comparison showing sustained lower A1c with metreleptin.

treatments/4.description: Recombinant leptin (metreleptin), used off-label, lowers HbA1c over long-term follow-up, likely through appetite suppression and reduced BMI rather than direct restoration of insulin signalling; lower BMI may worsen growth-hormone resistance.

evidence.snippet: Metreleptin alters the natural history of rising A1c in RMS, leading to lower A1c throughout long-term follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Documents durable A1c lowering with metreleptin.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Metreleptin lowers HbA1c via appetite suppression and reduced BMI.

evidence.explanation: States hormonal/antiandrogen management of hyperandrogenism.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies standard treatment for documented hypothyroidism.
